Generalised Linear Models: How the Pieces Fit Together

1 Introduction

An ecologist visits streams and records the number of salamanders seen. Another researcher weighs adult penguins and asks how body mass varies among species. A third wants to predict whether a survey will detect a species at all. Each has observations and predictors, but the observations do not have the same possible values. Counts are non-negative integers, detection is binary, and a measured body mass is positive and continuous. A model that ignores these distinctions may predict an impossible value or give uncertainty that does not describe the measurement process.

Generalised linear models, or GLMs, combine three decisions: a probability distribution for an observation, a systematic predictor built from its covariates, and a link connecting that predictor to the conditional mean. This primer explains why each decision exists, how the pieces determine a fit and its interpretation, and what to do when the assumptions fail. It begins with ordinary regression and concrete response models, derives the fitting machinery, and then develops uncertainty and model checking. Later sections develop overdispersion, dependence, smooth effects, multiple categories, zero processes, and Bayesian inference as responses to specific limitations.

The running setting is ecological monitoring, but no ecology background is required. A site is a location selected for study, a visit is a sampling occasion, and a detection means that an organism was recorded during that visit. A non-detection need not mean the organism was absent: an observer may miss it. Likewise, a recorded count need not equal the number present. We use small hypothetical calculations where the answer can be checked by hand, explicitly simulated examples where the generating mechanism is known, and separate real penguin and salamander studies. The real studies are not part of the simulated programme and should not be treated as causal experiments.

You should be comfortable with algebra, logarithms, elementary probability, derivatives, and the idea of a matrix. We refresh each tool as it becomes necessary. Read the main route in order: the later extensions build on problems exposed by the core models and return their results to the ecological question. R is the primary language. Complete examples and matched implementations in Python and Julia are described alongside the published example files; a code fragment is a teaching illustration unless its execution is recorded in the example manifest. The following cases use calculations and checks together.

The route moves from a question and ordinary regression to four response models, then asks why fitting works and how to assess its uncertainty. Count extensions follow a sequence of different discrepancies: variability, shared sites, nonlinear means and zeros. These components can coexist. The later combined case puts them together. The categorical and Bayesian chapters are optional branches for those response types and inferential questions; the synthesis returns to the decisions made along the way.

The cases do not all use the same observations. Penguins are a real positive-measurement study; Salamanders are a separate real repeated-count study. The Gamma holdout, the independent negative-binomial sample, the eight-site mixed-model illustration, the zero-process experiment and the combined monitoring survey are separately generated simulations. Their known mechanisms help diagnose a model; none establishes how the real studies were generated.

Keep a short analysis ledger as you read. For the penguins, the question is a species-specific mass mean and a future individual measurement; 342 rows supply both, while a sex comparison uses 333. For the real GP salamanders, a visit-level recorded count is nested in a site; the initial Poisson fit and later NB comparison use 92 visits at 23 sites, and prediction for a new site requires holding entire sites out. The independently simulated Gamma and count cases below have their own rows and validation splits. A result from one case is not a measurement from another.

1.1 Computation and Data Files

R carries the main narrative. The companion scripts in examples/ include matched R, Python and Julia implementations of the four core families, fixed-dispersion negative binomial fitting and a fixed-penalty spline. These are deliberately small algorithms checked against stated reference results; they are not replacements for general-purpose statistical software. More specialised examples use R. Package-specific snippets explicitly marked illustrative require their stated dependencies and are not covered merely because a different example passed.

The two real studies are separate from the synthetic monitoring programme. See data provenance for the frozen sources, reuse records and transformations, and example instructions for commands and execution limits. From the repository root, just examples glm runs the registered examples in the pinned containers. A registered example checks its particular calculation; it does not establish ecological adequacy or validate every formula in this document.

Verified against primary sources for cited dataset descriptions and statistical method and software reference summaries; unverified claims are flagged inline.

1.2 Notation

The table introduces the symbols used in the main route. Additional symbols are defined where needed; a subscript identifies an observation, not an exponent.

Symbol Meaning First Use
ii, nn Observation index and number of observations Sampling and regression
YiY_i, yiy_i Random response and its observed value Conditional mean
𝒙i\mathbf{x}_i, 𝑿\mathbf{X} Predictor vector for observation ii and design matrix Linear predictor
𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} Vector of regression coefficients Linear predictor
μi\mu_i Conditional mean of response ii Conditional mean
ηi\eta_i Linear predictor for observation ii GLM components
gg, g−1g^{-1} Link and inverse-link functions GLM components
ϕ\phi Dispersion parameter in a specified family Exponential family
θ\theta, bb, aa, cc Canonical parameter and functions in an exponential-family density Exponential family
ℓ\ell, 𝑼\mathbf{U}, 𝑰\mathbf{I} Log likelihood, score and expected information Fitting
𝑾\mathbf{W}, 𝒛\mathbf{z} Working weights and response for a fitting iteration IRLS
pip_i, mim_i Success probability and number of binomial trials Binary and grouped data
tit_i, rir_i Positive exposure and rate per exposure unit Count offsets
⋅̂\widehat{\cdot} Estimate computed from observed data Estimation
κ\kappa Negative-binomial shape, or explicitly declared fixed beta concentration Dispersion models / Bayesian hierarchy
𝒃\mathbf{b}, 𝑮\mathbf{G} Latent group effects and their covariance Multilevel models
λ\lambda, 𝑺\mathbf{S} Smoothing strength and penalty matrix Smooth effects
π\pi, qq Structural-zero mixture probability and hurdle positive-count probability Zero processes
KK, τk\tau_k Number of categories and ordered thresholds Categorical responses

Vectors and matrices are bold; the transpose 𝒙i⊤\mathbf{x}_i^{\top} turns a column vector into a row. We use log\log for the natural logarithm. A probability law is a model for uncertainty, not a promise that nature generated the data exactly according to that law.

2 From an Ecological Question to Regression

Before choosing a formula, identify what was sampled and what you want the model to say. A question about average recorded counts on future visits is different from a question about the number of animals present, and both differ from a claim that mining caused a change. The first may be described by a count regression; the second needs assumptions about detection; the third also needs a design or causal assumptions that address confounding.

2.1 Observations, Means, and Predictions

Let YiY_i be a response from a sampled unit with predictors 𝒙i\mathbf{x}_i. Its conditional mean is μi=E⁡(Yi∣𝒙i)\mu_i=\operatorname{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i): the average the model assigns to observations with those predictor values. An observed yiy_i is one realised value, not the mean itself. For a count, a fitted mean of 1.4 is a valid expectation even though no visit produces 1.4 salamanders. For binary detection, a mean of 0.7 is a modelled probability, not a prediction that a single observation will be 0.7.

The word conditional matters. If habitat and season both influence the response, the mean for one habitat at a specified season differs from an average over the mix of seasons in a population. State which population, site, visit, season, and measurement process your prediction concerns. A model may estimate an association within the observed sample and still fail to predict a different region or answer a question about an intervention.

Imagine that each independent site contributes one measured water-quality value and one salamander count. If the monitoring team selects easily accessible sites, an average over those sites need not represent remote streams. If the same site is visited four times, there are four observations but not four independent sites. The distinction affects both how much information the data provide and how we should split them for validation.

2.2 Ordinary Regression and Its Design Matrix

For a continuous response, ordinary linear regression starts with a mean that is linear in its coefficients. For example, with centred temperature xix_i and an indicator hih_i equal to one for a restored site and zero for a reference site, write

μi=β0+β1xi+β2hi+β3xihi. \mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\beta_2h_i+\beta_3x_i h_i.

Here the intercept is the reference-site mean at the centring temperature; β1\beta_1 is its temperature slope. The restored-site mean differs by β2\beta_2 at that temperature, and its slope is β1+β3\beta_1+\beta_3. The interaction does not say that the habitat difference is always β2\beta_2: it is β2+β3xi\beta_2+\beta_3x_i. Centring temperature changes the intercept and the point at which the habitat coefficient is interpreted, while preserving fitted values if the model is otherwise unchanged.

Suppose the coefficients are 10, 2, 3, and -0.5 in the units of the measurement. At xi=2x_i=2, the reference mean is 14 and the restored mean is 10+4+3−1=1610+4+3-1=16. The difference is 2, not 3. An interaction is useful when a scientific comparison may change with a predictor; it also requires data with enough overlap across predictor values to support that comparison.

The same model can be written μi=𝒙i⊤𝜷\mu_i=\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} with 𝒙i=(1,xi,hi,xihi)⊤\mathbf{x}_i=(1,x_i,h_i,x_i h_i)^{\top}. Stack rows to form the design matrix 𝑿\mathbf{X}. A categorical variable with three levels can be represented by an intercept and two indicator columns. The omitted level is the reference; choosing another reference changes the coefficients’ labels and values, not the fitted model space. A numerical code such as 1, 2, 3 would instead impose equal spacing and an ordering unless converted to categories.

Given a response vector 𝒚\mathbf{y}, ordinary least squares chooses coefficients to minimise ∥𝒚−𝑿𝜷∥2\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2. If 𝑿\mathbf{X} has full column rank, the normal equations are 𝑿⊤𝑿𝜷̂=𝑿⊤𝒚\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}. This equation explains the solution; in computation, a QR factorisation is generally preferable to explicitly inverting 𝑿⊤𝑿\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}, which can magnify conditioning problems. Rank deficiency means that at least one column is a linear combination of others: the data cannot distinguish every coefficient in the chosen parameterisation. Dropping a redundant column can yield estimable predictions for observed combinations, but it does not create information for an unobserved combination.

For conventional Gaussian regression we add Yi∣𝒙i∼N(μi,σ2)Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma^2) independently, with constant positive variance σ2\sigma^2. The mean model and the noise model make different promises. A least-squares fit can be computed without normality, but ordinary normal-theory intervals and likelihood comparisons require their respective assumptions or an appropriate alternative. A confidence interval for a mean reflects uncertainty about the fitted mean; a prediction interval for a new observation also includes variation around it. Even a perfectly known mean does not make future measurements identical.

Checkpoint. With the four-column design above, what is the row for a restored site at x=2x=2, and which number does it multiply to obtain the habitat difference? The row is (1,2,1,2)(1,2,1,2): its habitat terms contribute β2+2β3\beta_2+2\beta_3. If the coefficients were known exactly, that would determine the model mean, but a new measurement would still vary around it.

2.3 Three Levels and an Interaction in Rows

Suppose habitat has three categories: meadow, forest, and wetland, with meadow as reference. With continuous xx and a separate slope for each habitat, choose columns (1,x,Iforest,Iwetland,xIforest,xIwetland)(1,x,I_{\mathrm{forest}},I_{\mathrm{wetland}},xI_{\mathrm{forest}},xI_{\mathrm{wetland}}). The design rows for meadow at x=2x=2, forest at x=2x=2, and wetland at x=−1x=-1 are respectively

(1,2,0,0,0,0),(1,2,1,0,2,0),(1,−1,0,1,0,−1). (1,2,0,0,0,0),\quad(1,2,1,0,2,0),\quad(1,-1,0,1,0,-1).

For coefficients (10,2,3,−1,−0.5,1)(10,2,3,-1,-0.5,1), their mean predictors are 14, 16, and 6. The forest-minus-meadow difference at x=2x=2 is 3+2(−0.5)=23+2(-0.5)=2; at x=0x=0 it is 3. For a GLM these are contrasts on the link scale, not necessarily differences in outcome units. The three displayed rows alone cannot identify six coefficients: there must be sufficient data spanning predictor values within each category. Even with enough rows, a category seen only at one xx cannot identify its own slope separately from its intercept. A change of reference category produces another full-rank basis for the same model space when all relevant columns are estimable.

2.4 A Real Design: Penguin Mass

The Palmer penguin data contain adult measurements from three species and three islands. The packaged data come from work by Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research programme; the package authors provide source citations and reuse information. The source contains 344 records, of which 342 have body mass; sex is missing in 11 records, leaving 333 with both mass and sex. Missingness is information about the analysis, not a reason to quietly change the denominator.

On those 342 records, the observed species-by-island table has Adelie counts 44, 56, and 51 on Biscoe, Dream, and Torgersen; Chinstrap occurs only on Dream (68), and Gentoo only on Biscoe (123). An intercept, species, island, and all interactions create nine columns, but the matrix has rank five. Missing cells cannot support all nine coefficients. The additive species-plus-island matrix has rank five of five because the observed overlap connects the levels, but the fit still relies on the additive assumption and the particular observations. Full rank is not proof that species and island effects have been causally separated.

The following complete R example examines the intended rows and checks rank. The file is the frozen curated package dataset; paths are relative to this primer’s directory.

penguins <- read.csv("data/penguins.csv", na.strings = "NA")
penguins$species <- factor(penguins$species,
                           levels = c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"))
penguins$island <- factor(penguins$island,
                          levels = c("Biscoe", "Dream", "Torgersen"))
p <- subset(penguins, !is.na(body_mass_g) & !is.na(species))
stopifnot(nrow(p) == 342)
table(p$species, p$island)
X <- model.matrix(~ species * island, data = p)
c(rank = qr(X)$rank, columns = ncol(X))
g <- lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = p)
d <- p  # Same 342 analysis rows for later nested-model comparisons.
coef(g)

The fitted species means are approximately 3,701 g for Adelie, 3,733 g for Chinstrap, and 5,076 g for Gentoo. These describe the sampled adults under the stated model, not a controlled species experiment. Variation in sex, sampling, time, and location remains relevant. Later we compare a Gaussian and a Gamma model on exactly these same 342 rows rather than confusing a change of family with a change of sample.

The same 342 penguins with observed mass and species make the distinction between a confidence interval for a mean and a prediction interval for one new observation concrete. Use the fitted model g above, with Adelie as the reference, and request predictions at species = "Adelie". The fitted Adelie mean is 3,700.7 g. Under the model’s independent Gaussian errors with common variance, the 95% confidence interval for that population mean is approximately 3,626.7–3,774.7 g; the 95% prediction interval for one further Adelie penguin is 2,788.4–4,613.0 g. Both use the same fitted coefficients, residual standard deviation and 339 residual degrees of freedom. The second interval is much wider because it includes individual variation in addition to estimation uncertainty. These are model-based intervals for a comparable future observation, not evidence that all penguins in a wider population are represented by this sample.

new <- data.frame(species = factor("Adelie", levels = levels(d$species)))
predict(g, new, interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)
predict(g, new, interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)

The precision of the mean interval should not be mistaken for a narrow distribution of individual masses. The common Gaussian variance and independent sampling assumptions need scrutiny; uneven species–island coverage, missing values and the observational design limit generalisation. A new group, location, season or protocol could have additional variation not represented by this prediction interval.

The descriptive figure shows the sampled measurements before any regression fit.

3 How a Generalised Linear Model Fits Together

A GLM retains the design matrix and linear combination from ordinary regression, but it separates that combination from the mean and gives the response a distribution appropriate to its support. This division lets us ask what changes when we change the family, the link, or the predictors, instead of treating a named regression as an indivisible recipe.

3.1 From Design Row to Response Mean

For each observation, the systematic predictor is ηi=𝒙i⊤𝜷\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}, possibly with a known offset added. The response distribution describes the conditional variation around its mean μi\mu_i. The link relates the two:

g(μi)=ηi,μi=g−1(ηi). g(\mu_i)=\eta_i,\qquad \mu_i=g^{-1}(\eta_i).

Take a design row 𝒙=(1,2)⊤\mathbf{x}=(1,2)^{\top} and coefficients 𝜷=(−1,0.5)⊤\boldsymbol{\beta}=(-1,0.5)^{\top}. The linear predictor is −1+2(0.5)=0-1+2(0.5)=0. With a logit inverse link, the response mean is the detection probability 1/(1+e0)=0.51/(1+e^0)=0.5; with a log inverse link it is the expected count e0=1e^0=1. Now increase the covariate from 2 to 3, keeping the coefficients fixed. The new predictor is −1+3(0.5)=0.5-1+3(0.5)=0.5: the logit model gives probability e0.5/(1+e0.5)≈0.622e^{0.5}/(1+e^{0.5})\approx0.622, while the log-linked count model gives mean e0.5≈1.649e^{0.5}\approx1.649. The coefficient is the same change on the predictor scale, but the inverse link determines its interpretation on the response scale. These are illustrative fixed coefficients, not fitted ecological effects; an interaction or offset would change the calculation.

A Gaussian identity model has g(μ)=μg(\mu)=\mu and can assign any real mean. A Bernoulli logit model has g(μ)=log⁡{μ/(1−μ)}g(\mu)=\log\{\mu/(1-\mu)\} for a probability between zero and one. A Poisson log model uses g(μ)=log⁡μg(\mu)=\log\mu for a positive expected count. A Gamma log model also has a positive mean, but its continuous response and variance relationship differ from those of a Poisson count.

Consider the same numerical predictor η=1\eta=1 for two different observations. With a Bernoulli logit model the mean is a probability e/(1+e)≈0.731e/(1+e)\approx0.731; with a Poisson log model it is an expected count e≈2.718e\approx2.718. The same predictor value therefore has different meanings after the link is inverted. Even when two families share a log link, as Poisson and Gamma can, a mean of ee describes a non-negative integer count in one case and a positive continuous measurement in the other. Their conditional variances also differ: the Poisson variance is ee, while the Gamma variance is ϕe2\phi e^2. Choosing a link controls the mean scale; choosing a family adds assumptions about possible observations and their variation. Neither choice establishes that the covariates or sampling design are adequate.

The inverse links in the next figure show how the same predictor scale maps to different mean domains.

The linearity is in the predictor and coefficients, not necessarily in the response. A log-linked mean can curve exponentially as a covariate changes. A predictor may include a squared covariate, indicator, or interaction and remain linear in the coefficients. The inverse link transforms a mean; it does not transform a realised response and then assume ordinary errors. In particular, g{E⁡(Y∣X)}g\{\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X)\} is generally not E⁡{g(Y)∣X}\operatorname{E}\{g(Y)\mid X\}. We return to the practical consequences for positive measurements below.

3.2 What the Distribution Adds

The mean alone does not specify the possible outcomes or their spread. Hold the conditional mean at 0.50.5 in three models. A Bernoulli response can only be zero or one, with variance 0.5(1−0.5)=0.250.5(1-0.5)=0.25. A Poisson response can be any non-negative integer, with variance 0.50.5. A Gamma response is continuous and strictly positive, with variance ϕ(0.5)2=0.25ϕ\phi(0.5)^2=0.25\phi under the mean–dispersion parameterisation. For example, ϕ=2\phi=2 gives the Gamma the same variance as this Poisson, yet their supports and probabilities of individual outcomes differ: the Poisson can produce exactly zero and the Gamma cannot. Matching a mean, or even a mean and variance, does not make the distributions interchangeable.

The family supplies a probability model for outcomes around the mean; the link specifies how the mean changes with the predictor. A Poisson and a Gamma model can both use a log link, but a log-linked mean by itself does not decide whether the observation is a count or a positive measurement. Conversely, the same family can use different valid links, giving different mean curves. The family assumptions must be checked against the observation process and data; a compatible support alone does not establish the proposed variance, independence, or adequacy of the model.

The distribution and link are separate choices, although not every pairing is valid for every range of predictors. The canonical link makes the linear predictor equal to the exponential family’s canonical parameter under its chosen parameterisation. It is useful for algebra and computation, not a requirement that makes every other link invalid or scientifically inferior. For example, Bernoulli’s canonical logit and the noncanonical probit both map probabilities to a real-valued predictor; they imply different response curves.

4 Probabilities, Counts, and Exposure

A probability model should respect what each row records. Is it one visit, ten trials, a count in a fixed period, or a rate observed for varying lengths of time? The answer determines the denominator and likelihood before a formula is fitted.

4.1 Binomial Observations and the Meaning of Odds

A Bernoulli observation is one zero-or-one trial. A binomial observation is the number of successes among mim_i trials with common conditional probability pip_i, under the model’s independent-trial assumption. Its conditional mean is mipim_i p_i and variance mipi(1−pi)m_i p_i(1-p_i). A measured fraction is not automatically binomial: a proportion of land cover, for example, need not be the result of a known count of exchangeable successes and failures. The trial count affects uncertainty even when two observed fractions are identical.

In logistic regression, a coefficient changes the log odds. If a probability is 0.2, its odds are 0.2/0.8=0.250.2/0.8=0.25. An odds ratio of two changes those odds to 0.5 and the probability to 0.5/(1+0.5)=1/30.5/(1+0.5)=1/3, not 0.4. At a baseline probability of 0.8, doubling the odds gives 8/98/9. The same odds ratio has a different absolute probability effect at each baseline. Report predicted probabilities and their contrast for specified covariates as well as coefficients when the reader’s question concerns risk or detection.

A binomial likelihood assumes the stated trials share the modelled probability and have the dependence structure assumed in the model. Four repeat visits at one site can share weather, habitat, and unmeasured occupancy; four detections are not necessarily independent Bernoulli trials. A detection model concerns what the survey records. Inferring true occupancy requires a distinct observation process and identifying assumptions; a zero in a visit is not proof of absence.

4.2 A Binomial Likelihood You Can Calculate

Suppose a simple, deliberately idealised survey has eight independent visits under the same conditions, and three visits produce a detection. If the detection probability is pp, the binomial likelihood is proportional to p3(1−p)5p^3(1-p)^5; the binomial coefficient describes the number of sequences with three successes but does not depend on pp. At p=0.375p=0.375, this probability model has its largest likelihood. To see why, differentiate the log likelihood 3log⁡p+5log⁡(1−p)3\log p+5\log(1-p): its score is 3/p−5/(1−p)3/p-5/(1-p), which vanishes at p=3/8p=3/8. The second derivative is negative inside the unit interval. The data do not determine the probability without uncertainty: another set of eight visits would usually have a different count.

Now compare three detections in eight visits with 30 in 80. Both have the same maximum-likelihood estimate, 0.375. The second experiment has more information under the independent, equal-probability binomial model. Treating both fractions as equally precise discards their denominators. Conversely, multiplying a count of visits by ten on paper does not create information: if the visits are correlated or the 80 records contain repeated measurements of the same sites, the independent-trial likelihood can overstate the effective information. The data collection unit and dependence assumptions must travel with the denominator.

The following model uses successes and failures as two columns. Each row is one hypothetical group of independent visits with a shared probability; an observation of two successes from four visits contributes a different likelihood from one success in two, even though both fractions are one half.

trials <- data.frame(
  habitat = factor(c("reference", "reference", "restored", "restored")),
  successes = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  visits = c(4, 4, 4, 4)
)
trials$failures <- trials$visits - trials$successes
binomial_fit <- glm(cbind(successes, failures) ~ habitat,
                    family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = trials)
predict(binomial_fit, type = "response")

This is a syntax and arithmetic example, not a real study or a test of independence. The implied estimates are 3/8 for the reference group and 7/8 for the restored group. The first group’s odds are 3/53/5; the second group’s odds are 77. Their fitted odds ratio is 35/335/3, even though the probability difference is one half. With only two group probabilities and two coefficients, the fitted means reproduce the group fractions exactly. Uncertainty and assessment of the equal-probability and independence assumptions remain essential.

Checkpoint. The grouped data above contain three detections in eight reference visits. If a second dataset had 30 detections in 80 independent comparable visits, both sample fractions would be 0.375, but the latter likelihood is more concentrated. The denominator records information only if those are distinct, conditionally independent trials.

4.3 Poisson Counts and a Worked Offset

The following distributions show how the Poisson count probabilities change as the mean increases.

For a Poisson observation, the mean and variance are both μi\mu_i under the model. With a log link, increasing a predictor by one unit multiplies the conditional mean by eβje^{\beta_j} when other terms are fixed. If an interaction includes that predictor, its effect also depends on the interacting values. The support is a non-negative integer, but support alone does not establish a Poisson variance or independence.

Suppose an illustrative monitoring protocol records counts over different positive durations tit_i. If a constant within-visit rate is rir_i, then the expected count is μi=tiri\mu_i=t_i r_i. A log-linked rate regression therefore has

log⁡μi=log⁡ti+𝒙i⊤𝜷. \log\mu_i=\log t_i+\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}.

The term log⁡ti\log t_i is an offset: its coefficient is fixed at one, not estimated. If two visits have the same rate of 0.4 detections per hour but last two and five hours, their expected counts are 0.8 and 2.0. A comparison of raw counts would obscure their equal modelled rates. The proportionality assumption matters: doubling duration must double the expected count after conditioning on predictors. Fatigue, depletion, changing conditions, or variable detectability can violate it. Zero duration cannot be logged and usually contains no count exposure; negative duration is invalid. Model the actual effort and its units, and test the plausibility of proportionality rather than inventing a duration for a dataset that lacks one.

The following synthetic example simulates an explicit Poisson law, fixes a seed, and fits a log-rate model. It demonstrates syntax; its particular printed values are not evidence about any real survey.

set.seed(467)
survey <- data.frame(
  habitat = factor(rep(c("reference", "restored"), each = 40)),
  hours = rep(c(1, 2, 3, 4), 20)
)
survey$count <- rpois(nrow(survey), survey$hours *
                        ifelse(survey$habitat == "restored", 1.5, 1))
count_fit <- glm(count ~ habitat + offset(log(hours)),
                 family = poisson(link = "log"), data = survey)
summary(count_fit)
exp(coef(count_fit))

The intercept’s exponent is a rate for the reference habitat in the chosen unit; the other exponent is a rate ratio. A new visit’s expected count requires both its predicted rate and its duration. To forecast an actual count, include the assumed count distribution and uncertainty in fitted parameters; a confidence interval for the rate is not itself a prediction interval for the count.

Checkpoint. Two visits of one and four hours have the same expected rate of 0.8 recorded events per hour. Their expected counts are 0.8 and 3.2. The second is four times the first because the offset assumes proportionality to recorded effort; it is not evidence that detection is constant within a visit.

4.4 A Poisson Likelihood and Its Assumptions

Suppose independent counts yiy_i are observed at equal known exposure and the model assigns all of them the same Poisson mean μ\mu. Leaving the factorial terms visible, the log likelihood is ∑i{yilog⁡μ−μ−log⁡(yi!)}\sum_i\{y_i\log\mu-\mu-\log(y_i!)\}. Its derivative is ∑iyi/μ−n\sum_i y_i/\mu-n, so an interior maximum has μ̂=∑iyi/n\widehat\mu=\sum_i y_i/n. Thus the sample mean is not an arbitrary summary here: it is the maximum-likelihood estimate under this particular model. If all counts are zero, the maximum occurs at the boundary μ=0\mu=0; a finite log-mean parameter does not attain it, although it can approach it.

With unequal known exposure, the intercept-only rate estimate is total events divided by total exposure. For instance, counts 1 and 3 over one and three hours give a fitted rate of one event per hour, not the unweighted mean of the two observed hourly rates by accident or convention. With covariates the fitted rate changes across observations, and the corresponding coefficient score must be solved jointly. If effort is unknown, replacing it with an assumed constant can confound rate with time spent looking.

A Poisson model can arise from a constant-rate process with independent increments, but ecological counts may violate these conditions through aggregation, dependence, varying detection, or unobserved habitat differences. A good fit to the average does not prove the underlying event process.

5 Positive Measurements and the Meaning of a Transformation

A positive measurement calls for a choice about both the response distribution and the quantity being modelled. We first compare a Gamma mean model with regression on transformed measurements, then examine the Gamma density and its implications.

5.1 Gamma and Log-Transformed Measurements

A positive continuous outcome can have variability that grows with its mean. A Gamma model is one way to represent that pattern; it is not justified simply because all values happen to be positive. Its conditional density is supported on positive values. In a common mean–dispersion parameterisation, Var⁡(Yi∣𝒙i)=ϕμi2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\phi\mu_i^2 for ϕ>0\phi>0. A log link sets μi=exp⁡(𝒙i⊤𝜷)\mu_i=\exp(\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}). A one-unit coefficient change multiplies the conditional arithmetic mean by eβje^{\beta_j}, subject to interactions and the other terms being fixed.

Contrast this with fitting an ordinary Gaussian regression to log⁡Y\log Y. That model describes the mean of the transformed outcome, E⁡(log⁡Y∣X)\operatorname{E}(\log Y\mid X), rather than the log of its arithmetic mean. If log⁡Y\log Y is normal with conditional mean mm and variance s2s^2, then E⁡(Y∣X)=em+s2/2\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X)=e^{m+s^2/2}, while eme^m is the conditional median. For m=0m=0 and s2=1s^2=1, those are approximately 1.649 and 1. The nonlinearity of the exponential causes the distinction; Jensen’s inequality tells us that transforming an average and averaging transformed values need not agree. If the log-scale variance changes with covariates, a single retransformation factor is not generally adequate. A Gamma/log fit and a lognormal fit both preserve positive support but specify different distributions, variance structures, and interpretations.

Return to p, the same 342 penguins prepared in the regression section. Fit Gaussian identity and Gamma log with the same species predictor; the data do not change when the family changes:

normal_mass <- glm(body_mass_g ~ species, family = gaussian(), data = p)
gamma_mass <- glm(body_mass_g ~ species, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = p)
new_species <- data.frame(species = factor(c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"),
                                         levels = levels(p$species)))
data.frame(species = as.character(new_species$species),
      gaussian_g = predict(normal_mass, new_species, type = "response"),
      gamma_g = predict(gamma_mass, new_species, type = "response"))

Both fits reproduce the three group means here because the species-only predictor supplies one mean per species. Equal fitted means do not make their assumptions, likelihoods, residuals, or prediction intervals the same. The Gaussian fit’s estimated residual standard deviation is about 462 g; the Gamma dispersion estimate is about 0.0124 in the stated variance parameterisation. Neither result by itself selects a family. A check of residual behaviour, influential individuals, and predictive performance is needed. If sex is added, use the explicitly defined 333 complete records for both candidate models or explain why their samples differ. In that subset a Gaussian additive model estimates a male-minus-female difference of about 668 g conditional on species; a Gamma/log fit estimates a male log ratio of 0.159, or a mean ratio of about 1.17. The different scales answer different questions, and neither coefficient alone establishes a causal effect of sex.

A Gamma response cannot include exact zeros. A recorded zero could represent a true value, censoring below a detection limit, rounding, or a separate process; the scientific distinction determines a defensible model. Adding an arbitrary constant solely to make a logarithm work changes the model and the question. A two-part model may be useful for some zero-plus-positive outcomes, but a data-processing trick does not establish a two-process mechanism.

Checkpoint. Under a lognormal measurement model with m=0m=0 and s2=1s^2=1, exponentiating the mean log measurement gives the median, 1; the arithmetic mean is e1/2≈1.649e^{1/2}\approx1.649. This correction requires the assumed conditional lognormal model. A Gamma/log model links its arithmetic mean directly and makes a different variance claim.

5.2 The Gamma Density and Its Consequences

For a positive response, choose shape k=1/ϕk=1/\phi and scale ϕμ\phi\mu, with both ϕ\phi and μ\mu positive. The density at y>0y>0 is

f(y∣μ,ϕ)=y1/ϕ−1e−y/(ϕμ)Γ(1/ϕ)(ϕμ)1/ϕ. f(y\mid\mu,\phi)=\frac{y^{1/\phi-1}e^{-y/(\phi\mu)}}{\Gamma(1/\phi)(\phi\mu)^{1/\phi}}.

The shape and scale imply mean μ\mu and variance ϕμ2\phi\mu^2. If a hypothetical fitted mean is 10 g and ϕ=0.25\phi=0.25, the shape is 4, the scale is 2.5 g, the variance is 25 square grams, and the response standard deviation is 5 g. If a log-linked coefficient is log⁡2\log 2 for a one-unit predictor increase, the mean doubles to 20 g, the variance becomes 100 square grams, and the response standard deviation becomes 10 g. This relative spread follows from the model; it is a testable modelling implication, not a physical law. A coefficient uncertainty interval would add uncertainty about the mean, while these response standard deviations condition on fixed parameters.

The next figure compares two positive-response distributions with the same first two moments.

In the standard exponential-family representation the natural parameter is −1/μ-1/\mu with scale ϕ\phi, so the canonical relationship is an inverse mean with a sign determined by convention. Software often calls the positive reciprocal 1/μ1/\mu an inverse link; an unconstrained linear predictor under either sign must still give an admissible positive mean. The log link is noncanonical but maps every real predictor to a positive mean, and its coefficients express multiplicative changes. A fit with the log link still maximises the Gamma likelihood for its specified shape and mean; the link does not transform each observed mass into a Gaussian outcome.

For a fixed dispersion, the density says how a proposed mean assigns relative support to each positive measurement. Fitting the mean and dispersion uses all observations, not only whether they are positive. A diagnostic should compare the implied mean-dependent spread and tail with observations, consider measurement precision and zero mechanisms, and examine whether independent observations are plausible. A Gamma model can fit the mean adequately while misrepresenting its tails or vice versa. The R family documentation specifies the supported link choices and implementation conventions.

The independently simulated diagnostic and held-out repair below return to this Gamma mean and variance model.

Checkpoint. A positive response has conditional mean μ=4\mu=4. A Poisson law is a model for an integer count with variance 4; Gamma with ϕ=0.25\phi=0.25 is a model for a positive continuous measurement with variance 0.25(42)=40.25(4^2)=4. Matching the first two moments at one mean does not make their support or density the same. A log link can be used for either conditional mean; it does not make their observations interchangeable.

The matched fixed-design calculations for the four core families are available in R, Python and Julia. They compare bounded calculations on common inputs; the translations are teaching algorithms, not a claim of equivalent production package fits.

6 Likelihood, Fitting, and the Working Least-Squares Step

The binomial example chose p=3/8p=3/8 because it gave the observed result the greatest likelihood. A regression makes the same choice jointly for coefficients: a model becomes a fitted model when data are used to choose its unknown parameters. The likelihood measures the relative support that the specified probability model assigns to different parameter values for the observed data. It is a function of the parameters with the observations held fixed; it is not, by itself, a probability distribution over parameters.

6.1 Why the Exponential Family Is Useful

A conventional GLM uses a response distribution expressible in an exponential-family form. For a scalar observation, write its probability mass or density as

f(yi;θi,ϕ)=exp⁡{yiθi−b(θi)a(ϕ)+c(yi,ϕ)}. f(y_i;\theta_i,\phi)=\exp\left\{\frac{y_i\theta_i-b(\theta_i)}{a(\phi)}+c(y_i,\phi)\right\}.

Here θi\theta_i is a canonical parameter, ϕ\phi is a dispersion parameter where the family has one, and aa, bb, and cc are functions chosen for the distribution and parameterisation. Known prior weights can change the denominator; we use the common unweighted form for this derivation. The formula covers densities and probability masses with respect to an appropriate base measure; it does not say a continuous density is itself a probability at one exact value.

Assume the support does not depend on θi\theta_i and differentiation can pass through the normalising integral or sum. Differentiating the log density gives the score for θi\theta_i, (yi−b′(θi))/a(ϕ)(y_i-b'(\theta_i))/a(\phi). Its expectation is zero under the model, so μi=b′(θi)\mu_i=b'(\theta_i). A second differentiation, or the score variance identity under the same regularity conditions, gives Var⁡(Yi)=a(ϕ)b″(θi)\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=a(\phi)b''(\theta_i). This is the mechanism by which a family supplies a mean–variance relationship. It is not a general formula for arbitrary distributions or non-regular support.

To see the first identity rather than memorise it, the log-density derivative is (y−b′(θ))/a(ϕ)(y-b'(\theta))/a(\phi). The integral of the density is one for each admissible θ\theta; differentiating that identity under the stated regularity conditions gives an expected score of zero. Therefore E(Y)−b′(θ)=0E(Y)-b'(\theta)=0. Differentiating again gives expected negative curvature b″(θ)/a(ϕ)b''(\theta)/a(\phi); equating it to the score variance gives Var⁡(Y)/a(ϕ)2=b″(θ)/a(ϕ)\operatorname{Var}(Y)/a(\phi)^2=b''(\theta)/a(\phi). The assumption about exchanging differentiation and integration is doing real work here.

For a Poisson observation, θ=log⁡μ\theta=\log\mu, b(θ)=eθb(\theta)=e^\theta, and a(ϕ)=1a(\phi)=1. Thus both mean and variance are eθ=μe^\theta=\mu. The canonical link is the log. For a Bernoulli observation, θ=log⁡{p/(1−p)}\theta=\log\{p/(1-p)\} and b(θ)=log⁡(1+eθ)b(\theta)=\log(1+e^\theta), giving mean pp and variance p(1−p)p(1-p). The Gaussian family with fixed variance has an identity canonical link. A Gamma distribution can also be put in exponential-family form; its canonical link is an inverse-mean form, whereas the log link used in the positive-response example is noncanonical and often convenient for multiplicative interpretation. A scale factor and sign convention must be stated when comparing canonical parameter definitions.

A distribution’s variance relationship is a model restriction. If observed counts vary substantially more than the Poisson model predicts, a Poisson mean may still be useful, but its likelihood-based uncertainty and predictive distribution may be misleading. Dispersion models examine quasi-likelihood and negative binomial alternatives; multilevel models address a different possible source of variation, shared site effects. These explanations can coexist, so checking one does not automatically settle the other.

6.2 From Likelihood to Score and Information

For independent observations with fitted means determined by coefficients, multiply their model probabilities or densities. The log likelihood ℓ(𝜷)\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) converts that product to a sum. Maximum likelihood chooses a parameter value that maximises the sum, provided a finite, identifiable maximum exists. The score 𝑼=∂ℓ/∂𝜷\mathbf{U}=\partial\ell/\partial\boldsymbol{\beta} is its gradient; the expected information 𝑰\mathbf{I} is the negative expected Hessian, measuring local curvature under regularity conditions. Near a well-behaved maximum, more curvature generally means more information about a parameter combination. It does not protect against confounding, a wrong model, or a maximum at infinity.

For independent Bernoulli observations with canonical logit, pi=1/(1+e−𝒙i⊤𝜷)p_i=1/(1+e^{-\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}}). Ignoring no terms that depend on the coefficients, the log likelihood, score, and expected information are

ℓ=∑i{yilog⁡pi+(1−yi)log⁡(1−pi)},𝑼=𝑿⊤(𝒚−𝒑),𝑰=𝑿⊤𝑾𝑿, \ell=\sum_i\{y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\},\quad \mathbf{U}=\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{p}),\quad \mathbf{I}=\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X},

where 𝑾\mathbf{W} is diagonal with entries pi(1−pi)p_i(1-p_i). The score compares observed outcomes with fitted probabilities, multiplied by the design columns. The weights are largest at probability one half and approach zero near either boundary. For the canonical Bernoulli logit, this expected information is also the observed negative Hessian. Other family–link combinations need not have that equality.

6.3 One Logistic IRLS Iteration by Hand

Consider four independent hypothetical binary detections. The first two have x=0x=0, the second two x=1x=1, and the outcomes are (0,1,1,1)(0,1,1,1). Fit an intercept and slope, starting both coefficients at zero. Every initial predictor is zero and every initial probability is one half. With rows (1,xi)(1,x_i), the score is (1,1)⊤(1,1)^{\top}: one more success was observed overall than the two expected, and one more success was observed in the x=1x=1 group than the one expected.

Each initial weight is 1/41/4. Therefore the information matrix and its inverse are

𝑰=(11/21/21/2),𝑰−1=(2−2−24). \mathbf{I}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{I}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}.

The Fisher-scoring update adds 𝑰−1𝑼=(0,2)⊤\mathbf{I}^{-1}\mathbf{U}=(0,2)^{\top} to the old coefficients. After one step the intercept is zero and the slope is two, giving fitted probabilities 0.5 at x=0x=0 and approximately 0.881 at x=1x=1. This is an iteration, not the final fit. All observed x=1x=1 responses are successes; in this tiny example the unpenalised slope has no finite maximum, so repeated iterations do not settle on a finite estimate. A numerical stopping message alone cannot repair that statistical boundary.

The same update is a weighted least-squares calculation. At a current iterate, define the working response zi=ηi+(yi−pi)/{pi(1−pi)}z_i=\eta_i+(y_i-p_i)/\{p_i(1-p_i)\}. Here it is (−2,2,2,2)(-2,2,2,2) and each weight is 1/41/4. Regressing these working responses on the intercept and xx with those weights yields the same new coefficients (0,2)⊤(0,2)^{\top}. The algorithm updates the probabilities, weights, and working responses, then repeats: hence iteratively reweighted least squares, or IRLS. The working response is an algebraic device on the predictor scale; it is not a newly observed biological measurement. Small weights near zero or one explain why extreme fitted probabilities can make curvature weak and estimation unstable.

More generally, with a differentiable inverse link and conditional variance Var⁡(Yi)=ϕV(μi)\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\phi V(\mu_i), the working response is zi=ηi+(yi−μi)/(dμi/dηi)z_i=\eta_i+(y_i-\mu_i)/(d\mu_i/d\eta_i) and weights are proportional to (dμi/dηi)2/{ϕV(μi)}(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)^2/\{\phi V(\mu_i)\}. These formulae require a nonzero derivative and finite, valid variance at the current mean. In practice, use a stable linear solve, inspect convergence and rank, and recognise that a noncanonical link can make a Newton step differ from Fisher scoring. The original GLM formulation connects exponential-family responses and iterative weighted regression; see Nelder and Wedderburn and the R glm documentation.

The working weights are not arbitrary importance scores. They follow from the way a change in a coefficient changes the mean and thus the likelihood. For independent observations in the unweighted exponential-family form above, take a(ϕ)=ϕa(\phi)=\phi and write V(μi)=b″(θi)V(\mu_i)=b''(\theta_i). The chain rule gives dμi/dθi=V(μi)d\mu_i/d\theta_i=V(\mu_i) and dηi/dβj=xijd\eta_i/d\beta_j=x_{ij}. Consequently the score for coefficient jj is

Uj=∑ixijyi−μiϕV(μi)dμidηi. U_j=\sum_i x_{ij}\frac{y_i-\mu_i}{\phi V(\mu_i)}\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}.

The expected information follows from the covariance of these scores under the independent model. In matrix form it is 𝑿⊤𝑾𝑿\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}, with wi=(dμi/dηi)2/{ϕV(μi)}w_i=(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)^2/\{\phi V(\mu_i)\}. The weight increases where changing the predictor moves the mean substantially relative to its variance. It does not mean an individual is more valuable, and it changes as the fitted means change. Known observation weights and binomial denominators need their own representation; do not multiply by a trial count twice.

Let a known offset be oio_i, so ηi=oi+𝒙i⊤𝜷\eta_i=o_i+\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}. Fisher scoring solves 𝑿⊤𝑾𝑿Δ𝜷=𝑼\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\beta}=\mathbf{U} and sets the new coefficients to the old ones plus Δ𝜷\Delta\boldsymbol{\beta}. Defining zi=ηi+(yi−μi)/(dμi/dηi)z_i=\eta_i+(y_i-\mu_i)/(d\mu_i/d\eta_i) converts the update into the working weighted least-squares normal equations

𝑿⊤𝑾𝑿𝜷new=𝑿⊤𝑾(𝒛−𝒐). \mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}} =\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{o}).

The known offset remains in the working predictor; it is subtracted from the working response when solving for the free coefficients. It is never fitted as another free column. The same equations can be solved with a stable weighted QR factorisation without explicitly forming an inverse. An iterate may require step control or fail to exist if the matrix is singular.

The bridge to weighted least squares follows by substituting z−η=(y−μ)/(dμ/dη)z-\eta=(y-\mu)/(d\mu/d\eta) into X⊤W(z−η)X^{\top}W(z-\eta). With the stated weights this is the score, so X⊤WXΔβ=UX^{\top}WX\Delta\beta=U becomes X⊤WXβnew=X⊤W(z−o)X^{\top}WX\beta_{\mathrm{new}}=X^{\top}W(z-o). In the four-observation example, z=(−2,2,2,2)z=(-2,2,2,2) and W=I/4W=I/4. The two columns of XX sum the weighted working responses to (1,1)(1,1); solving the previously displayed information system yields (0,2)(0,2). This is the same first scoring step, not a second fit to new observations.

Checkpoint. If two grouped rows have the same fraction and current probability but the second has twice as many independent trials, their working responses are the same. Its weight doubles: under the binomial assumptions the larger denominator supplies more information, not a different observed proportion.

For a Gaussian identity model, dμ/dη=1d\mu/d\eta=1 and V=1V=1, giving constant weight 1/ϕ1/\phi. For a Bernoulli logit model, dμ/dη=p(1−p)d\mu/d\eta=p(1-p) and V=p(1−p)V=p(1-p), giving p(1−p)p(1-p). For a Poisson log model, both derivative and variance function are μ\mu, giving weight μ\mu. For Gamma/log with variance ϕμ2\phi\mu^2, the derivative is μ\mu and the weight is the constant 1/ϕ1/\phi. These apply to individual observations under the specified parameterisations. A common positive multiplier in all weights does not change a weighted least-squares coefficient update, but dispersion still affects uncertainty.

For a grouped binomial row with m=10m=10, observed success fraction 0.70.7, and current probability p=0.4p=0.4, use the fraction as response and its variance p(1−p)/mp(1-p)/m. The working response is logit⁡(0.4)+(0.7−0.4)/(0.4⋅0.6)≈0.8445\operatorname{logit}(0.4)+(0.7-0.4)/(0.4\cdot0.6)\approx0.8445, and its weight is mp(1−p)=2.4m p(1-p)=2.4. A second row with the same observed fraction and m=20m=20 has the same working response but weight 4.8. These weights encode independent trials with a common probability, not a guarantee that the trials were actually independent.

6.4 Separation and Penalisation

If predictors perfectly separate successes from failures, coefficients can diverge while fitted probabilities approach zero or one. This is a property of the unpenalised likelihood, not evidence for a scientifically infinite effect. Near separation, a finite but very large estimate and standard error can be just as misleading. Examine cross-tabulations, coefficient magnitude, warnings, and fitted probabilities rather than checking only whether the solver stopped.

One remedy changes the objective by adding a penalty. For example, maximise ℓ(𝜷)−λ∑j≥1βj2/2\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta})-\lambda\sum_{j\geq1}\beta_j^2/2 with λ>0\lambda>0, leaving the intercept unpenalised if the implementation does so. The penalty discourages large slopes and can produce a finite estimate in a separated example, subject to the treatment of the intercept and data. It changes the estimator and objective, generally introduces regularisation bias, and requires a tuning decision; the scientific estimand need not change. Select the penalty within the training process, not on the final test set. Standard unpenalised confidence intervals do not automatically apply to a penalised estimate. Alternative bias-reduction methods and explicit Bayesian priors are different approaches, not synonyms for the same penalty; Bayesian models make the prior assumption visible.

Consider a related separated example: ten observations have x=0x=0, with four successes and six failures, and ten have x=1x=1, all successes. With an intercept and slope, the finite group probability at x=0x=0 is 0.4, while increasing the slope drives the probability at x=1x=1 towards one and continues to improve the unpenalised likelihood. Fitting with a maximum of 15 iterations gives a slope near 16.97; allowing 25 gives about 19.97 and predicted probabilities approximately 0.4 and 0.999999997. Software’s numerical stopping rule can declare convergence even though the mathematical maximum occurs only at an infinite slope. The exact coefficient printed depends on numerical tolerance, not an identified finite effect.

For a concrete repair, minimise the negative Bernoulli log likelihood plus λ(β02+β12)/2\lambda(\beta_0^2+\beta_1^2)/2, explicitly penalising the intercept as well as the slope in this illustration. With λ=1\lambda=1, the fitted intercept is about 0.156 and slope 1.544, giving probabilities 0.539 and 0.846 at x=0x=0 and x=1x=1. This is a finite estimate because the penalty makes large coefficients costly; its probability is not the unpenalised maximum-likelihood answer. The intercept was included in the penalty here to make the objective explicit, though many implementations choose otherwise. With λ=0.25\lambda=0.25 the corresponding probabilities are about 0.471 and 0.932; with λ=4\lambda=4 they are 0.568 and 0.724. The strength and choice of regularisation matter substantially in this small separated sample. Select and validate the penalty according to the intended prediction task, ideally within training data; extra data or a justified prior are other possible routes.

x <- c(rep(0, 10), rep(1, 10))
y <- c(rep(0, 6), rep(1, 4), rep(1, 10))
X <- cbind(1, x)
unpenalised <- glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(),
                   control = glm.control(maxit = 25))
objective <- function(b, lambda) {
  eta <- drop(X %*% b)
  sum(log1p(exp(eta)) - y * eta) + lambda * sum(b * b) / 2
}
penalised <- optim(c(0, 0), objective, lambda = 1, method = "BFGS")
plogis(c(penalised$par[1], sum(penalised$par)))

The direct log1p(exp(eta)) calculation is sufficient for this bounded illustration but can overflow at extreme predictors; use a numerically stable loss and a validated implementation for production. Penalisation does not repair an unrepresentative sample, unmeasured confounding or a missing observation process.

7 Uncertainty, Prediction, and Model Comparison

A fit is the beginning of an analysis. We need to know which uncertainty is being reported, what evidence challenges the model, and whether a proposed repair answers the same scientific question. No single diagnostic converts a model into a fact.

7.1 Coefficients, Contrasts, and Intervals

A standard error describes variation in an estimator under a stated procedure and assumptions. Near a regular, identifiable maximum and with enough information, inverse information estimates coefficient covariance. A Wald interval adds and subtracts a critical multiple of the standard error on the coefficient scale. For a log-rate coefficient, exponentiating the interval endpoints produces an interval for a rate ratio; for a logit coefficient it produces an interval for an odds ratio. Neither directly gives an interval for an absolute difference in probability.

A response-scale prediction depends on all coefficients. For a scenario 𝒙\mathbf{x}, calculate the linear predictor and its covariance using the entire coefficient covariance matrix, then transform endpoints where a monotone inverse link makes that appropriate. For a contrast between two predictions, account for their shared estimated coefficients. Simulation from an approximate coefficient distribution or an appropriate bootstrap can carry a nonlinear contrast through the inverse link; neither replaces checking whether the approximations and resampling design are justified. Sampling sites as independent resampling units may be more appropriate than sampling individual visits when sites are the independent units.

A confidence interval is constructed by a procedure whose repeated-sampling coverage is defined under its assumptions. It is not a probability that a fixed parameter lies in the realised interval under ordinary frequentist interpretation. A prediction interval for a future observation also incorporates response variability and depends on the future unit, exposure, and distribution. For the salamanders, a future visit to an already sampled site and a visit to a new site can have different predictive uncertainties once site variation is modelled.

7.2 Tests and Model Comparisons

A Wald test divides an estimate by its standard error. A likelihood-ratio test compares twice the difference in maximised log likelihoods of nested models; its familiar reference distribution requires conditions such as comparable data, an appropriate likelihood, and regular parameters away from problematic boundaries. A variance component at zero, separation, small samples, or data-dependent selection can invalidate a routine reference approximation. State the hypothesis and assumptions, report an effect and uncertainty, and avoid interpreting a non-significant result as proof of no effect.

Deviance compares a fitted likelihood with a saturated benchmark under a defined family; its numerical meaning depends on the response and likelihood. AIC combines maximised log likelihood and a parameter-count penalty to estimate a relative predictive criterion under assumptions. Compare AIC only for models fitted to the same response observations using commensurable, fully specified likelihoods, including consistent treatment of normalising constants and transformations. A log-transformed response requires the appropriate Jacobian before likelihoods on different response scales can be compared. Quasi-likelihood does not supply an ordinary full probability likelihood and therefore does not supply an ordinary likelihood AIC. Neither a small AIC difference nor an isolated p-value establishes a biological mechanism.

Prediction can be a separate objective from coefficient inference. Choose the estimand, the relevant loss or score, and validation unit before optimising a metric. Mean absolute error is interpretable in response units but does not test an entire predictive distribution; a log score assesses probability assigned to the held-out realised value but is sensitive to extreme overconfident predictions. Report the score’s direction and handle zero assigned probabilities deliberately.

Returning to the penguin data d and fitted Gaussian model g, compare models on the same 342 rows. For a concrete nested likelihood comparison, compare the intercept-only Gaussian model with the species-means model. Both maximise their Gaussian likelihood including a common residual variance, and their log-likelihood degrees of freedom include that variance parameter. The species model adds two mean parameters: twice the fitted log-likelihood difference is 378.82, compared with a chi-squared reference distribution with two degrees of freedom, giving approximately p=5.5×10−83p=5.5\times10^{-83} under the usual likelihood-ratio approximation. In this sample, the common-mean model is very difficult to reconcile with the observed species differences under these model assumptions. This is not a test of whether species causes body-mass differences, nor does it validate a common variance or the sampling design.

g0 <- lm(body_mass_g ~ 1, data = d)
stopifnot(nobs(g0) == nobs(g))
LR <- 2 * as.numeric(logLik(g) - logLik(g0))
df <- attr(logLik(g), "df") - attr(logLik(g0), "df")
c(statistic = LR, df = df, p_value = pchisq(LR, df, lower.tail = FALSE))

Use the same observations and response scale, check that the models really are nested, and state the reference distribution’s regularity assumptions. If model choices were made by repeatedly inspecting these data, the nominal pp-value does not account for that selection. For these normal models a classical equal-variance nested F test is another available procedure; its finite-sample reference and statistic are not identical to the asymptotic likelihood-ratio calculation.

A numerical comparison needs the same underlying observations and probability measure. In the synthetic Poisson example below, the two log likelihoods include the same log⁡(y!)\log(y!) constants, the saturated likelihood is common, and Poisson dispersion is fixed at one. The deviance difference therefore equals twice the fitted log-likelihood difference. AIC adds 2k2k to negative twice the log likelihood, where kk is the number of independently estimated parameters. The comparison trades the extra parameter against the likelihood improvement; it does not turn a selected model into the data-generating truth.

For a Gaussian or Gamma likelihood, dispersion is ordinarily an estimated nuisance parameter as well as the regression coefficients. It must be counted and fitted consistently when calculating likelihoods and AIC; a residual degrees-of-freedom estimate and a maximum-likelihood dispersion estimate are not always the same. Do not manually compare a likelihood using one convention with an AIC generated under another without checking the implementation. R’s model-specific likelihood and AIC details are documented in logLik and AIC.

Suppose Z=log⁡YZ=\log Y has normal density fZf_Z and a competing model supplies a Gamma density for the original positive YY. The lognormal density on the original scale is fY(y)=fZ(log⁡y)/yf_Y(y)=f_Z(\log y)/y: the factor 1/y1/y is the Jacobian of the change of variable. Thus the log likelihood for observed original-scale values subtracts ∑ilog⁡yi\sum_i\log y_i from the Gaussian log likelihood computed for the logs. Omitting that term makes a nominal AIC comparison mix likelihoods for different measurement scales. The adjustment does not settle whether either model is appropriate, and a sample change caused by missing values remains a separate obstacle.

The usual chi-squared likelihood-ratio approximation can be unreliable for small samples, separated logistic data, and parameters on a boundary, such as a zero random-effect variance or a zero mixture weight. Penalised fits and quasi-likelihoods also require methods matched to their objectives. A suitable simulation or bootstrap under a clearly specified null can sometimes provide a reference distribution; this costs computation and inherits the null model assumptions. Do not apply a routine degrees-of-freedom rule to every comparison merely because software prints a deviance.

7.3 A Worked Covariance, Interval, and Prediction

Suppose a fitted logistic intercept and slope are −1-1 and 0.80.8, and their estimated covariance matrix is

𝚺̂=(0.04−0.015−0.0150.09). \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{pmatrix}0.04&-0.015\\-0.015&0.09\end{pmatrix}.

For the hypothetical prediction at x=2x=2, the linear predictor is −1+2(0.8)=0.6-1+2(0.8)=0.6. Its variance is (1,2)𝚺̂(1,2)⊤=0.04+4(0.09)+4(−0.015)=0.34(1,2)\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}(1,2)^{\top}=0.04+4(0.09)+4(-0.015)=0.34; the standard error is approximately 0.583. The off-diagonal covariance contributes -0.06. Ignoring it would give variance 0.40, and in another fit the covariance could have the opposite sign. For a slope contrast between x=2x=2 and x=1x=1, the intercept cancels, so the link-scale contrast is 0.8 with variance 0.09. These are different questions and use different contrast vectors.

A 95% normal-approximation interval on the first linear predictor is 0.6±1.96(0.583)0.6\pm1.96(0.583). Applying the logistic inverse link to its endpoints gives approximately 0.368 to 0.851, with point prediction 0.646. This transformation preserves the interval’s ordering and keeps it within the probability domain; its coverage still depends on the underlying approximation. The delta method instead uses the inverse-link derivative p(1−p)p(1-p) to obtain response-scale standard error 0.646(1−0.646)(0.583)≈0.1330.646(1-0.646)(0.583)\approx0.133. A symmetric response-scale normal interval would be about 0.384 to 0.907. It is not identical, and for a more extreme probability it can leave the valid range. Neither method is automatically reliable for separation or a small sample.

The following reproducible calculation also draws 20,000 coefficient vectors from the approximate normal sampling distribution with this covariance. Its 2.5% and 97.5% probability quantiles are about 0.368 and 0.850. This is a simulation of a normal approximation, not a nonparametric or parametric bootstrap refitting the original data.

beta <- c(-1, 0.8)
V <- matrix(c(0.04, -0.015, -0.015, 0.09), 2, 2)
new_x <- c(1, 2)
eta <- sum(new_x * beta)
se_eta <- sqrt(drop(t(new_x) %*% V %*% new_x))
p_hat <- plogis(eta)
c(estimate = p_hat, plogis(eta + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se_eta))
set.seed(467)
draws <- matrix(rnorm(40000), ncol = 2) %*% chol(V) +
  matrix(beta, nrow = 20000, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)
quantile(plogis(draws[, 1] + 2 * draws[, 2]), c(0.025, 0.975))

A genuine parametric bootstrap instead simulates a fresh response under a fitted sampling model, refits every simulated dataset, and recomputes the quantity. A nonparametric bootstrap resamples the sampled units and refits. Both expose fitting failures and may capture asymmetry missed by a normal approximation, but a parametric bootstrap inherits its generative assumptions and a nonparametric bootstrap must respect clusters and the original design. Compare the three approaches for the same target and record failed refits. With a fitted probability of 0.646, one future Bernoulli observation is either 0 or 1, with those model probabilities conditional on the fitted parameters; its conditional variance is about 0.229. The interval for the probability is not an interval asserting that a future binary observation will be between 0.368 and 0.851. For future data, account for both outcome variation and parameter uncertainty in a predictive distribution.

Interactions add another reason to work with a stated contrast rather than read a coefficient in isolation. Consider four independent groups of 100 simulated visits, one at each combination of x∈{0,1}x\in\{0,1\} and habitat indicator h∈{0,1}h\in\{0,1\}. Their observed detections are 20, 40, 55 and 85 in the order (x,h)=(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)(x,h)=(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1). Fit a grouped-binomial logit model with an intercept, both main effects and their interaction. The fitted probabilities in this saturated four-cell example are 0.20, 0.40, 0.55 and 0.85. This construction makes the calculations transparent; it does not establish an ecological effect or test goodness of fit because the model has one fitted probability per cell.

The estimated habitat log-odds contrast is 1.587 at x=0x=0 and 1.587+0.553=2.1401.587+0.553=2.140 at x=1x=1. On the probability scale, the habitat contrasts are 0.55−0.20=0.350.55-0.20=0.35 and 0.85−0.40=0.450.85-0.40=0.45, respectively: the difference of these differences is 0.10. The logit interaction is a change in log odds, whereas 0.10 is a change in probability differences for these particular covariates. Even with no logit-scale interaction, nonlinearity can yield a non-zero probability-scale difference of differences; neither quantity is a universal effect across baselines.

The two coefficients in the habitat contrast at x=1x=1 come from the same fitted model and are correlated. In this fit their estimated covariance is −0.1029-0.1029. The variance of their sum is approximately 0.1201 after including twice that covariance; adding only their separate variances gives 0.3259. Omitting covariance would materially change the uncertainty calculation. This is a link-scale contrast; obtaining an interval for a response-scale difference requires the joint coefficient covariance, for example with a delta-method gradient or joint coefficient draws, and the relevant approximation and sampling assumptions.

cells <- expand.grid(x = c(0, 1), habitat = c(0, 1))
cells$success <- c(20, 40, 55, 85)
cells$failure <- 100 - cells$success
m <- glm(cbind(success, failure) ~ x * habitat,
         family = binomial(), data = cells)
b <- coef(m)
V <- vcov(m)
prob <- predict(m, cells, type = "response")
c(contrast_x0 = prob[3] - prob[1], contrast_x1 = prob[4] - prob[2])
c(link_x1 = b["habitat"] + b["x:habitat"],
  variance_x1 = V["habitat", "habitat"] + V["x:habitat", "x:habitat"] +
    2 * V["habitat", "x:habitat"])

8 Diagnosing, Validating, and Revising Models

A model check becomes useful when it changes a decision: identify the target, inspect a discrepancy, revise a specified component, and evaluate the same target again. The Gamma example below uses independent simulated measurements; the real salamander visit example requires site-aware validation.

8.1 Residuals, Calibration, and Influence

A raw residual is yi−μ̂iy_i-\widehat\mu_i. A Pearson residual divides this difference by the modelled standard deviation, while a deviance residual relates an observation’s likelihood to a saturated fit under the family. They answer related but different questions. Plot residuals against fitted means, important covariates, time, and site where meaningful; look for nonlinearity, unequal variability, clusters, outliers, or systematic residual patterns. Discrete outcomes do not yield a continuous normal residual cloud even under a correct model. Simulated residual or posterior-predictive comparisons can make discrete distributions easier to assess, but depend on the model and simulation scheme.

For a probability model, calibration compares predicted probabilities with observed frequencies across suitable groups or through a calibration model. If all visits predicted near 0.7 contain detections around 70% of the time in a representative validation sample, that is evidence about calibration in that sample, not a guarantee for every site or subgroup. Calibration alone does not prove good discrimination, useful decisions, or correct causal interpretation. For counts, compare observed and simulated count distributions, zeros, dispersion, and patterns by site and exposure, not just the overall mean.

Influence asks whether an observation or cluster materially changes a result when removed or perturbed. A large residual need not be influential if its predictor is ordinary; a high-leverage point may have a small residual but determine a slope. Check data quality, then perform sensitivity analyses at the unit that could be influential, such as the site rather than one repeated visit. Removing inconvenient observations without a documented reason is not diagnosis. If a biologically real observation changes the conclusion, report the sensitivity and consider whether the model or the data collection needs improvement.

8.2 Numerical Residuals and Calibration

For an illustrative Poisson observation with count y=5y=5 and fitted mean μ=2\mu=2, the Pearson residual is (5−2)/2≈2.121(5-2)/\sqrt{2}\approx2.121. The signed deviance residual is

sign⁡(y−μ)2{ylog⁡(y/μ)−(y−μ)}≈1.778. \operatorname{sign}(y-\mu)\sqrt{2\{y\log(y/\mu)-(y-\mu)\}}\approx1.778.

It comes from twice the log-likelihood difference between a saturated model with mean yy and the fitted mean; the factorial terms cancel. For y=0y=0, define ylog⁡(y/μ)y\log(y/\mu) by its limit zero. The total deviance is the sum of squared deviance residuals; Pearson residual squares instead scale raw differences by fitted variances. Neither should be treated as a normal z-score without a justified approximation, particularly for small fitted counts.

Suppose a held-out detection model gives ten visits probabilities near 0.2 and ten near 0.8. If the first group contains two detections and the second contains seven, the observed bin frequencies are 0.2 and 0.7, compared with average predicted probabilities near 0.2 and 0.8. This is a small illustrative calibration table, not strong evidence of calibration: bin boundaries and the sampling variability of ten trials matter, and visits sharing a site are not independent replicates. Inspect the distribution of predictions, report bin sizes and uncertainty, and use held-out data or a suitable grouped cross-validation scheme. A calibration curve or intercept and slope can avoid an arbitrary small number of bins, but also needs enough data and a declared validation population.

Influence is a change in a result, so calculate it on the target scale. Suppose a fitted rate ratio is 1.40 using all sites and 1.05 after removing one site. The 0.35 change in that contrast is a sensitivity result, not a reason by itself to remove the site. Check recording errors, compare site characteristics, repeat the analysis with a suitable site-level model, and show both results if the observation is valid. The values here are hypothetical; no such deletion analysis has been claimed for the salamander data.

8.3 A Diagnostic, Repair, and Re-Evaluation

This seeded simulation supplies a known nonlinear Poisson mean. The initial log-linear model omits the quadratic term; the repair includes it. Both are fitted to the same 40 synthetic observations, eight at each predictor value. We inspect mean raw residuals at each value before and after the change and compare likelihoods; we do not select the repair by repeatedly searching many candidate models.

set.seed(467)
x <- rep(0:4, each = 8)
y <- rpois(length(x), exp(0.25 + 0.15 * x + 0.2 * x^2))
survey <- data.frame(x, y)
linear <- glm(y ~ x, family = poisson(), data = survey)
curved <- glm(y ~ x + I(x^2), family = poisson(), data = survey)
aggregate(residuals(linear, type = "response") ~ x, survey, mean)
aggregate(residuals(curved, type = "response") ~ x, survey, mean)
c(linear_logLik = as.numeric(logLik(linear)),
  curved_logLik = as.numeric(logLik(curved)),
  linear_deviance = deviance(linear), curved_deviance = deviance(curved),
  linear_AIC = AIC(linear), curved_AIC = AIC(curved))

The linear fit’s mean raw residuals at x=0,1,2,3,4x=0,1,2,3,4 are approximately 1.102, 0.000, -0.875, -2.660, and 2.432. Their systematic pattern is a reason to inspect the mean function. After adding the prespecified quadratic, they are 0.278, -0.485, -0.214, 0.771, and -0.350; the remaining fluctuations are not all zero. The log likelihoods are -99.835 and -90.830, and residual deviances are 64.708 and 46.698. The likelihood-ratio statistic is 2(−90.830+99.835)=18.0102(-90.830+99.835)=18.010, also the deviance difference because the saturated reference and observed data are identical. The quadratic model uses one additional coefficient; its AIC is 187.660 versus 203.670 for the linear model, using 2 and 3 free regression coefficients respectively. Under regular large-sample and independent-Poisson assumptions a one-degree-of-freedom likelihood-ratio reference is a possible approximation, but this constructed example is primarily a diagnostic demonstration.

The source mechanism was defined as quadratic, so a model that includes it can recover the correct mean form in expectation; the realised sample still contains Poisson noise. Improved in-sample deviance does not establish out-of-sample performance or the correctness of a real ecological mechanism. Re-evaluate with independently simulated or held-out units, inspect dispersion and influential points, and use site-blocked validation if the observational design includes repeated sites. The example has no site structure and cannot test that concern.

8.4 Validation and Selection

A model intended for future observations at known sites poses a different validation task from prediction at new sites. A random row split can put visits from the same site in both sets. It may be suitable for a precisely defined within-site target, but it does not test transport to an unseen site. A grouped split holds complete sites out; temporal blocking may be needed for future years, and spatial blocking may be needed for new regions. Estimate preprocessing, imputation, transformations, and tuning on training data only, then apply them to validation data without looking at its responses.

For the real GP salamander case, define the target as recorded counts at new sites under a comparable survey protocol. Reserve whole sites as a final test set before fitting; keep all visits from each reserved site together. Within the remaining sites, use grouped folds to choose among prespecified model structures or tuning settings. In each fold, estimate any imputation or transformation from the fold’s training sites, fit the candidate there, and apply those choices to the validation sites. Compare predictions at the site level using a declared score and inspect count, zero and site-total discrepancies; for a shared-site model, the joint predictive distribution must retain the shared effect. Select the procedure using these folds, refit it on all non-test sites, then evaluate once on the held-out sites. Record the split and uncertainty: with only 23 sites, results may be sensitive to which sites are held out. This is a proposed workflow for the real case, not a claim that these calculations were performed or that a single split establishes transport to other regions.

8.5 Missing Data and Model Revision

Complete-case analysis is easy to run and can be appropriate under particular assumptions, but it changes the analysed population if missingness depends on measurements, response, or unobserved values. In the penguin example, adding sex reduces the analysis from 342 mass records to 333 complete records. Compare models on the same defined sample when comparing fits, describe who was excluded, and investigate the pattern of missingness. Imputation, weighting, sensitivity analysis, or collecting better measurements may be appropriate, but each requires assumptions and a method suited to the design; replacing a missing value with zero silently asserts a measurement that was not made.
