A useful modelling ledger records the question, sampling unit, response, predictor and variance assumptions, diagnostic concern, chosen change, and what happened after re-evaluation. If count residuals reveal site clustering, a negative-binomial variance adjustment alone does not necessarily address correlation; if the mean is nonlinear, inflating a standard error does not repair the mean. Add a site model or smooth only when the design and question justify it, then repeat the checks and state the limits that remain. See smooth effects, zero processes, and categorical responses for further changes to the model.

The next case has a different role from the penguin analysis. Its generated data supply a known mean function, so we can tell whether an apparent repair addresses the constructed mistake. The training and held-out observations below are independent synthetic units, not penguins or salamander visits.

8.6 A Gamma Mean Repair and Its Remaining Uncertainty

The penguin fit illustrates a real positive response; a separate simulation lets us know which structural mistake generated a diagnostic pattern. Generate 400 independent positive measurements with xx uniformly distributed on [−1,1][-1,1], conditional mean μ(x)=exp⁡(1+1.1x)\mu(x)=\exp(1+1.1x) and a Gamma shape of 4. This implies conditional variance μ2/4\mu^2/4. The fixed-seed script uses the first 250 observations for training and the remaining 150 for a held-out check; this random independent split is appropriate only for the simulated independent units, not automatically for repeated ecological sites.

Start with a Gamma/log model containing only an intercept. On the held-out observations, the mean residual is −1.52-1.52 for x≤0x\leq0 and 1.281.28 for x>0x>0: the one-mean model systematically overpredicts the first group and underpredicts the second. This discrepancy points to the missing gradient, not necessarily to the Gamma variance assumption.

Add the already observed xx as a linear term in the log mean and refit using the same training set. The fitted intercept and slope are 0.968 and 1.076, respectively; held-out group mean residuals become 0.13 and −0.21-0.21.

The held-out mean negative log predictive density changes from 2.033 to 1.645, and mean absolute error from 1.920 to 1.227. Smaller is better for both scores. Here the known generating mean includes xx; improvement in one simulated split does not establish that adding a variable will improve an unrelated real-data analysis.

The apparent repair is incomplete. Construct 95% plug-in observation intervals from each fitted Gamma distribution using its fitted mean and estimated dispersion. In this test set they cover 98.0% of observations for the intercept-only model and 89.3% for the model with xx.

The wider misspecified model happens to cover more observations, while its log score and residual pattern are worse. Neither a single coverage percentage nor one log score establishes calibration. The refitted model’s estimated dispersion is 0.190 versus the generating value 0.25; uncertainty in dispersion and sampling variation are not included in the plug-in interval. A wider validation sample, diagnostics of the conditional distribution and assessment of dispersion uncertainty are needed before interpreting its 95% label as reliable.

At x=0.8x=0.8, the revised model’s estimated mean is 6.225 in the simulation’s measurement units.

A 500-replicate parametric bootstrap resimulates the training responses under that fitted Gamma model, refits both mean and dispersion and, for each successful refit, simulates one future observation at x=0.8x=0.8. The approximate percentile interval for the estimated mean is 5.657–6.826; the simulated future-observation interval is 1.974–12.547. No refits failed in this particular run. These intervals use the same fitted model and target covariate, but answer different questions: the future value adds outcome variation. The bootstrap assumes the fitted Gamma model is the generator, and 500 replicates make tail endpoints noisy; report failed refits, check Monte Carlo stability and do not treat this conditional illustration as a validated coverage guarantee.

set.seed(222468)
n <- 400
x <- runif(n, -1, 1)
y <- rgamma(n, shape = 4, scale = exp(1 + 1.1 * x) / 4)
train <- data.frame(x = x[1:250], y = y[1:250])
test <- data.frame(x = x[251:400], y = y[251:400])
m0 <- glm(y ~ 1, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = train)
m1 <- glm(y ~ x, family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = train)
mu <- predict(m1, newdata = test, type = "response")
shape <- 1 / summary(m1)$dispersion
bounds <- cbind(qgamma(0.025, shape, scale = mu / shape),
                qgamma(0.975, shape, scale = mu / shape))
mean(test$y >= bounds[, 1] & test$y <= bounds[, 2])

The displayed code takes the revised training fit through the held-out interval check. The other reported diagnostics require the companion script: first compute predictions for both models on the identical test rows, then aggregate residuals within the two gradient ranges and score the held-out responses. The bootstrap instead repeatedly regenerates training responses, refits, and predicts at the stated x=0.8x=0.8; it is a distinct operation from calculating the plug-in bounds.

The complete examples/core-repairs.R adds the baseline comparison, both scores, the group residual calculation and the fixed-seed bootstrap. It records the complete result, including failed refits; the displayed fragment shows the held-out interval calculation and does not by itself reproduce the bootstrap endpoints.

9 When Counts Vary More Than the Poisson Model Allows

A Poisson regression makes two claims, not one: the conditional mean is linked to the predictors, and the conditional variance equals that mean. A sensible fitted mean does not guarantee the second claim. Ecological counts can vary because sites differ in unmeasured habitat, animals cluster, survey conditions change, observations share a site, or the recording process creates extra zeros. These explanations do not all imply the same repair. Here we separate a limited claim about the mean and its uncertainty from a complete probability model for counts. The distinction matters when the goal changes from estimating a rate ratio to predicting how many zeros or very large counts a future survey will produce.

For this chapter let YiY_i be the count at observation ii, μi=E(Yi∣xi)\mu_i=E(Y_i\mid x_i), and log⁡μi=xi⊤β+log⁡ei\log\mu_i=x_i^{\top}\beta+\log e_i, where ei>0e_i>0 is known exposure. The offset constrains a doubling of exposure to double the expected count, an assumption worth checking. Conditional means and variances refer to observations with the same covariates and exposure, not the raw mean and variance of a heterogeneous dataset. A raw variance exceeding its mean can arise even when every conditional Poisson assumption is correct.

The separate fixed-shape NB comparison has matched implementations in R, Python and Julia. These isolate the count family and parameterisation; they do not fit the later site-and-smooth model.

9.1 Real Repeated Counts and a First Diagnostic

The glmmTMB Salamanders documentation describes repeated stream counts from the Price and colleagues study and cites its Dryad data. Our frozen file is derived from the identified package object, not asserted byte-identical to the original Dryad file. It records 23 sites, four visits, seven species or life-stage labels, mining status, and scaled sampling covariates. The package documentation identifies DOP as scaled days since precipitation; a unit change in this field is not necessarily one day.

Select the prespecified GP group: 92 observations, four per site, with 12 reference and 11 mined sites. A Poisson model of recorded count on mining status and scaled DOP, ignoring site dependence for this initial illustration, gives a mined coefficient about -3.881. At DOP = 0 its fitted means are about 2.206 observations per visit at reference sites and 0.0455 at mined sites. These are fitted observed counts under the model and observed sampling conditions, not estimates of true abundance or proof of a causal mining effect. The severe imbalance in observed counts and repeated visits make both uncertainty and model adequacy important.

salamanders <- read.csv("data/salamanders-package.csv")
gp <- subset(salamanders, spp == "GP")
gp$mined <- factor(gp$mined, levels = c("no", "yes"))
stopifnot(nrow(gp) == 92, length(unique(gp$site)) == 23)
fit_gp <- glm(count ~ mined + DOP, family = poisson(), data = gp)
summary(fit_gp)
new_sites <- data.frame(mined = factor(c("no", "yes"),
                                      levels = levels(gp$mined)),
                        DOP = 0)
predict(fit_gp, newdata = new_sites, type = "response")
sum(residuals(fit_gp, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(fit_gp)

The Pearson residual sum of squares divided by residual degrees of freedom is approximately 2.147 in this fit. It is a warning to investigate, not a proof of a particular mechanism or a complete diagnostic test. Extra variation, site dependence, an incorrect mean function, unmodelled detection, and other mismatches can all matter. Dispersion models and multilevel models return to distinct possible responses. No survey-effort offset has been invented for these data.

For our real GP data, the sample variance of recorded counts is about 4.98 in reference sites while its sample mean is about 2.21; mined sites have much smaller recorded values. This simple grouping is not a model-based test of conditional overdispersion because the observations have different covariates and repeated sites. It does explain why comparing observed and model-predicted variation is a sensible next step.

In the preliminary GP salamander example, one seeded split of 24 test rows shared all 17 test sites with training. Another held out six whole sites, also 24 rows. Poisson mean absolute error was 0.708 for the row split and 1.185 for the held-site split. These are different test observations and only one split: the contrast illustrates the change in target, not a general estimate of bias or proof that a site-blocked score must be worse. Repeated, suitably grouped validation and uncertainty across splits would be needed for a stronger performance claim. The initial fit has no site random effect, but shared site conditions can still make row-level validation unrepresentative of new sites.

9.2 Detecting a Discrepancy and Choosing Its Target

Fit the Poisson model, inspect residuals against predictors, fitted means, site and time, and compare observed features with simulated datasets from the fitted model. A common descriptive statistic is

ϕ̂P=1n−p∑i=1n(yi−μ̂i)2μ̂i, \widehat\phi_P=\frac{1}{n-p}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(y_i-\widehat\mu_i)^2}{\widehat\mu_i},

where pp is the rank of the fitted mean model, including the intercept, and n−pn-p is its residual degrees of freedom. Values appreciably above one can flag excess conditional variation, but a threshold does not identify its cause. A wrong mean, outlier, dependence or omitted offset can produce the same signal. It is also possible to have a statistic near one while a specific feature, such as zero frequency, is badly predicted. Inspect the sampling design before adding a dispersion parameter.

Suppose the residual Pearson sum of squares is 180 for 90 residual degrees of freedom. Then ϕ̂P=2\widehat\phi_P=2. Under the assumptions below, a quasi-Poisson standard error is approximately 2\sqrt 2 times its Poisson counterpart: a coefficient with standard error 0.10 has one of about 0.141. The estimated coefficient and its rate ratio do not change in this particular Poisson-versus-quasi-Poisson comparison, but the reported uncertainty does. This arithmetic assumes the same data, predictors, weights and log link, and a common scale; it does not repair dependence or a biased mean.

9.3 Quasi-Likelihood: A Variance Relationship, Not a Count Distribution

A quasi-Poisson model asserts E(Yi∣xi)=μiE(Y_i\mid x_i)=\mu_i and Var⁡(Yi∣xi)=ϕμi\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid x_i)=\phi\mu_i, with common ϕ>0\phi>0, without specifying every count probability. For independent observations, the estimating equation for a log link is proportional to

U(β)=∑ixi(yi−μi)=0. U(\beta)=\sum_i x_i(y_i-\mu_i)=0.

The common factor 1/ϕ1/\phi does not alter its root. That is why glm(..., family = quasipoisson) and the corresponding Poisson fit have the same coefficients, subject to numerical tolerance. The scale estimate multiplies the model-based covariance, whose standard errors therefore change by its square root. The relation between mean and variance is an assumption across the range of fitted means, and the mean model and independence still matter. Wedderburn’s quasi-likelihood formulation builds inference from a mean–variance relationship rather than requiring a full likelihood.

A sandwich covariance takes a different route. Let uiu_i be an observation’s estimating-function contribution and AA the derivative-based sensitivity matrix. A schematic estimate has the form Â−1(∑iuiui⊤)Â−⊤\widehat A^{-1}(\sum_i u_i u_i^{\top})\widehat A^{-\top}. Its middle term uses observed score variation instead of requiring a single correctly specified proportional scale. If observations are dependent within sites, sum uiu_i within each site before forming the outer products; the independent units are then sites, and few sites make the asymptotic approximation precarious. A sandwich covariance does not cure a misspecified mean, informative selection or lack of independent clusters. It can differ substantially from the quasi scale estimate; neither is a synonym for the other.

Because quasi-Poisson alone assigns no probability to each possible count, it does not supply an ordinary log likelihood, ordinary likelihood-ratio test, ordinary AIC or a full predictive distribution. R returns NA for its AIC. Do not simulate future counts by quietly assuming a Poisson distribution with inflated standard errors: that reintroduces a distribution whose variance is wrong. For mean inference, inspect residuals and uncertainty under the assumptions chosen; for probabilities of zeros or extremes, specify and check a complete distribution.

9.4 Negative Binomial: A Complete Alternative

A negative-binomial model supplies such a distribution. For the NB2 convention with shape κ>0\kappa>0,

P(Y=y)=Γ(y+κ)Γ(κ)y!(κκ+μ)κ(μκ+μ)y,y=0,1,…,E(Y)=μ,Var⁡(Y)=μ+μ2κ. \begin{aligned} P(Y=y)&=\frac{\Gamma(y+\kappa)}{\Gamma(\kappa)y!} \left(\frac{\kappa}{\kappa+\mu}\right)^\kappa \left(\frac{\mu}{\kappa+\mu}\right)^y,\quad y=0,1,\ldots,\\ E(Y)&=\mu,\quad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mu+\frac{\mu^2}{\kappa}. \end{aligned}

The following distributions share a mean but differ in their predicted zeros and upper tails.

One explanation is a Poisson count with a random rate Λ\Lambda, where Λ\Lambda is Gamma distributed with mean μ\mu and variance μ2/κ\mu^2/\kappa. The law of total variance gives E(Λ)+Var⁡(Λ)E(\Lambda)+\operatorname{Var}(\Lambda), the expression above. This is one generative construction, not evidence that the underlying ecological rate is Gamma distributed. As κ→∞\kappa\to\infty, extra variance vanishes and NB2 approaches Poisson. At μ=4\mu=4 and κ=2\kappa=2, variance is 4+16/2=124+16/2=12, and P(Y=0)=(2/6)2=1/9P(Y=0)=(2/6)^2=1/9, compared with e−4≈0.0183e^{-4}\approx0.0183 under Poisson. A larger zero frequency can therefore arise from ordinary rate heterogeneity without a separate zero-producing class.

NB1 is different. One convention has Var⁡(Y)=μ(1+α)\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mu(1+\alpha), α≥0\alpha\geq0, while NB2 has quadratic extra variance. At μ=2\mu=2 and α=1\alpha=1, NB1 variance is 4; at μ=4\mu=4 it is 8. NB2 with κ=2\kappa=2 gives 4 and 12 respectively. These match at one mean but not across the range. Software names and dispersion directions differ: in the glmmTMB family reference, its NB1 dispersion increases extra variance, whereas its NB2 dispersion is the denominator of the quadratic term. MASS::glm.nb calls the NB2 shape theta; here we write κ\kappa to distinguish it from the exponential-family canonical parameter. Read the actual variance formula before transferring a coefficient between packages.

MASS::glm.nb alternates between estimating regression coefficients for a given shape and estimating the shape from the likelihood given the current fitted means; iteration continues towards a joint fit. The likelihood includes the normalising terms involving κ\kappa, so changing shape affects more than a variance multiplier. Check convergence, profile or otherwise assess shape uncertainty, and recognise that a very large estimate can indicate a likelihood nearly flat towards the Poisson limit. A finite printed estimate does not ensure that shape is well determined. NB2 supplies a likelihood and hence likelihood-based AIC for comparable fits to the same response observations, provided the fitted likelihoods and constants are comparable. The estimated shape is a fitted parameter and belongs in the parameter count; software normally handles this. AIC compares relative expected predictive performance under its assumptions, not biological truth. NB2 is not automatically the best model when variance exceeds the Poisson mean: dependence, a misspecified mean or a detection process can remain.

9.5 Simulated Comparison and a Real-Data Boundary

The following deliberately generates independent NB2 observations. It is a demonstration of a known simulation mechanism, not an ecological claim. MASS is a recommended R package. The fixed seed makes the generated sample reproducible within the stated R environment; print results from the actual run rather than taking the generating parameters as fitted estimates.

set.seed(46705)
n <- 400
x <- runif(n, -1, 1)
effort <- runif(n, 0.5, 2)
mu <- effort * exp(0.4 + 0.7 * x)
y <- rnbinom(n, mu = mu, size = 2)
d <- data.frame(y, x, effort)
p <- glm(y ~ x + offset(log(effort)), poisson, data = d)
q <- update(p, family = quasipoisson)
nb <- MASS::glm.nb(y ~ x + offset(log(effort)), data = d)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(coef(p), coef(q), tolerance = 1e-6)))
cbind(Poisson = coef(summary(p))[, 2], quasi = coef(summary(q))[, 2],
      NB2 = coef(summary(nb))[, 2])
c(scale = summary(q)$dispersion, shape = nb$theta,
  poisson_AIC = AIC(p), NB2_AIC = AIC(nb), quasi_AIC = AIC(q))
# Compare observable zero counts to draws from each complete fitted model.
B <- 1000
zero_p <- replicate(B, sum(rpois(n, fitted(p)) == 0))
zero_nb <- replicate(B, sum(rnbinom(n, mu = fitted(nb), size = nb$theta) == 0))
rbind(observed = sum(y == 0), Poisson = quantile(zero_p, c(.025, .5, .975)),
      NB2 = quantile(zero_nb, c(.025, .5, .975)))

In the pinned R 4.5.3 runtime this seed gives Poisson and NB2 slope estimates 0.6694 and 0.6228 (rate ratios about 1.953 and 1.864). Their model-based slope standard errors are 0.0655 and 0.0955; quasi-Poisson has the Poisson slope and standard error 0.0949 with estimated scale 2.0944. NB2 estimates κ=1.6373\kappa=1.6373, compared with the generating value 2; this is an estimate, not a known parameter, and its uncertainty should be examined. Poisson AIC is 1567.61, NB2 AIC 1440.76, and quasi AIC is unavailable. There are 136 observed zeros, compared with conditional simulated central 95% ranges 70–100 for Poisson and 112–147 for NB2. Thus Poisson badly misses this particular feature; NB2 is consistent with it in this check. This does not establish that its full distribution is correct.

For a numerical contrast with a sandwich, artificially group adjacent observations in pairs, calculate Poisson score contributions ui=xi(yi−μ̂i)u_i=x_i(y_i-\widehat\mu_i) and sum them within each pair, then use the sensitivity A=X⊤diag⁡(μ̂)XA=X^{\top}\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\mu)X. The resulting uncorrected cluster-sandwich slope standard error is 0.0990, versus 0.0949 from the common quasi scale. These pairs were independently generated and are an arithmetic illustration, not evidence of real clustering. With real shared sites, cluster by site and assess the number of independent sites; finite-cluster corrections and the choice of asymptotic reference distribution matter. The numerical difference is sample-specific: sandwich is not guaranteed to be larger. Both approaches require a correctly specified mean for the intended coefficient interpretation.

The final rbind recycles the single observed value across three columns, allowing direct comparison with the simulated 2.5%, median and 97.5% summaries. These simulations condition on fitted parameters: they do not include parameter uncertainty, and a fitted model can pass this one check while failing another. Also compare residuals against x and effort and check calibration beyond the features examined below. If the quasi scale changes with μ\mu, a single ϕ\phi is inadequate even if its average seems plausible.

The earlier zero simulation used all 400 observations to fit and check the model; the next calculation changes the question to prediction on observations the model did not see. Retain the same synthetic input and randomly reserve 100 of the 400 independent observations before fitting either model. Define the upper tail in advance as counts of at least five, and simulate 3,000 held-out datasets at the test rows’ observed covariates and efforts, using the training fits. The held-out sample contains 33 zeros and four counts of at least five. Poisson’s simulated central 95% ranges are 11–24 zeros and 6–17 upper-tail counts; NB2’s are 21–38 zeros and 8–22 upper-tail counts. The revision improves the zero check but overpredicts this particular upper tail even more.

Its mean held-out log probability is −1.651 per observation, versus −1.749 for Poisson: better aggregate predictive score does not mean every feature is calibrated. The fitted NB2 shape from the 300 training observations is 1.526. The chosen tail threshold, one random split and random simulation variation affect the result. These ranges condition on fitted parameters; they omit estimation uncertainty. This deliberately independent construction justifies a row split; use held-out sites when predicting new sites. Investigate the mean and the distribution, repeat with independent samples or suitable validation, and do not infer a biological mechanism from either score.

The complete reproducible calculation is in examples/extensions-bayes-repairs.R.

The bounded real-data calculations are also available in R, Python and Julia. The Python and Julia translations check the stated fixed-design real-data fits; they do not estimate a site random effect or detection process.

The package-derived Salamanders data provide a useful counterexample to assuming independence. In a preliminary fit of the 92 observations for species GP, four visits at each of 23 sites were treated as independent. With count ~ mined + DOP and unmined as reference, the Poisson and NB2 estimates of the mined log rate ratio were approximately -3.881 and -3.873; the estimated NB2 shape was 1.731. These are associations in recorded counts, not causal effects or estimates of occupancy. Pearson sums of squares divided by residual degrees of freedom were about 2.147 and 1.408 respectively, but neither statistic establishes adequacy, and both fits ignore shared sites. DOP is scaled days since precipitation, not raw days; there is no invented survey-effort or detection measure here. The next chapter addresses site dependence. The observations and their provenance are described in the data documentation accompanying this primer.

Try it. Change the simulated NB2 shape to 0.5 and then 20. Compare the estimated rate ratio, quasi standard error, fitted shape and zero simulations. Why can a change in the variance model change NB coefficients but not quasi-Poisson coefficients? Now simulate site-specific effects and compare the result of a row split with a site split; which prediction target does each split approximate?

Outline answer. A smaller NB2 shape increases variance relative to its mean, while a larger shape approaches Poisson variation. NB maximum-likelihood coefficients can change because the likelihood weights observations differently; quasi-Poisson with one common scale leaves the Poisson mean score unchanged. A row split targets another visit from represented sites, while a site split tests prediction for held-out sites; neither split repairs an incorrect observation process.

10 Repeated Sites and Generalised Linear Mixed Models

Repeated surveys of the same pond are not independent replicates of ponds. They may share water chemistry, vegetation, survey access and animals. Treating every visit as an unrelated site can make a dataset appear more informative about the population of sites than it is. A generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) represents some dependence through latent site effects. It is an extension of a GLM: the conditional response distribution and link are GLM-like, but the likelihood for the observed data integrates over unobserved effects. Its extra structure answers a question about how sites vary; it also adds assumptions that a large number of visits at only a few sites cannot validate by itself.

10.1 A Model for Visits Within Sites

Let YijY_{ij} be the recorded count on visit jj to site ii, and xijx_{ij} a measured covariate. A random-intercept Poisson model is

Yij∣bi,xij∼Poisson⁡(μij),log⁡μij=β0+β1xij+bi,bi∼iidN(0,σb2). Y_{ij}\mid b_i,x_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_{ij}),\qquad \log\mu_{ij}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_i,\qquad b_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim N(0,\sigma_b^2).

Conditional on bib_i and the covariates, visits are independent in this model. Marginally, visits at the same site are dependent because they share bib_i. A site whose latent intercept is high tends to have higher counts on all its visits. Different sites are independent under the stated model. Neither a random intercept nor a negative-binomial response automatically handles seasonal serial correlation, spatial dependence between nearby sites, changing detection or omitted predictors.

The random effects are assumed independent across sites and independent of the covariate process under this formulation; their covariance matrix must be positive semidefinite. If site characteristics affect both bib_i and xijx_{ij}, this independence assumption and the corresponding interpretation can fail. A random slope allows the relationship with xx to vary by site:

log⁡μij=β0+β1xij+b0i+b1ixij,(b0ib1i)∼N((00),(σ02σ01σ01σ12)). \log\mu_{ij}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_{0i}+b_{1i}x_{ij},\quad \binom{b_{0i}}{b_{1i}}\sim N\!\left(\binom00, \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_0^2&\sigma_{01}\\\sigma_{01}&\sigma_1^2\end{pmatrix}\right).

Site-specific intercepts and slopes require replication and variation in xx within sites. If xx is constant within every site, its site-specific slope cannot be separated in the same way from a site intercept. Centre a continuous xx at a meaningful value: the random intercept and its correlation with the slope then refer to that value. A fixed site factor estimates an unrelated coefficient for each observed site; random effects instead posit a population distribution and allow predictions for new sites under that distribution. Neither choice removes confounding by variables that differ between sites.

10.2 Partial Pooling and Prediction Targets

For a transparent calculation, temporarily use a Gaussian measurement model: y‾i∣bi∼N(bi,4/ni)\bar y_i\mid b_i\sim N(b_i, 4/n_i) and bi∼N(0,1)b_i\sim N(0,1), with both variances fixed and known. If a site has ni=1n_i=1 observation with y‾i=2\bar y_i=2, its unpooled estimate is 2 and its posterior mean is [1/(1+4)]2=0.4[1/(1+4)]2=0.4. With ni=16n_i=16 and the same average, the posterior mean is [1/(1+4/16)]2=1.6[1/(1+4/16)]2=1.6. Both are pulled towards zero, but the more informative site is pulled less. These are conditional estimates under the stated Gaussian model; real GLMM pooling is nonlinear and variance parameters are estimated, so those exact weights do not apply.

The random-effects distribution pulls weakly informed site estimates towards the population centre. This partial pooling is not an arbitrary adjustment: site data and the population distribution both enter the conditional distribution of bib_i. A site with many informative visits can depart more strongly from zero than one with few, all else equal. Shrinkage depends on the estimated variance and observation model. It improves stability only if the assumed exchangeable population is appropriate.

With β0=log⁡2\beta_0=\log 2, β1=log⁡1.5\beta_1=\log 1.5, and σb2=0.5\sigma_b^2=0.5, consider x=1x=1. The conditional mean for a site with b=0b=0 is 2×1.5=32\times1.5=3. At a site with b=log⁡2b=\log 2, it is 6. For a randomly selected new site, averaging over bb yields

E(Y∣x=1)=3E(eb)=3e0.5/2≈3.852. E(Y\mid x=1)=3E(e^b)=3e^{0.5/2}\approx3.852.

The zero-effect site is therefore not the population average on the response scale. This is a consequence of the nonlinear inverse link, not a numerical quirk. For an observed site, a plug-in prediction at its estimated bib_i is conditional on that estimate; integrating over uncertainty in bib_i gives a different prediction. For a new site, one can report the population-average mean, or simulate a new bb and count to describe a future site’s predictive distribution. The latter includes between-site and count variation; uncertainty in fitted parameters adds another layer. With random slopes, the marginal mean becomes exp⁡(x⊤β+z⊤Σz/2)\exp(x^{\top}\beta+z^{\top}\Sigma z/2), where zz contains the random-effect covariates. Thus even the shape of a marginal effect may differ from its conditional counterpart.

10.3 Fitting Integrates Over What Was Not Observed

For independent sites, the observed-data likelihood is

L(β,σb)=∏i∫−∞∞[∏jp(yij∣bi,β)]φ(bi;0,σb2)dbi. L(\beta,\sigma_b)=\prod_i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left[\prod_j p(y_{ij}\mid b_i,\beta)\right] \varphi(b_i;0,\sigma_b^2)\,db_i.

The inner product uses the conditional count density; the integral averages it over possible latent effects. Maximising a conditional likelihood after treating each estimated bib_i as known is not this marginal likelihood. Except in special cases the integrals have no closed form. Laplace approximation uses a local quadratic approximation near the integrand’s mode; adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature evaluates strategically chosen points and can be more accurate for low-dimensional integrals at higher cost. Approximation quality depends on the data and model. Compare feasible settings and examine convergence, rather than treating a successful optimiser message as validation. The lme4 GLMM vignette develops these approximations and their computational trade-offs.

The fitted variance can sit at zero, a boundary where ordinary interior normal and chi-square approximations may fail. A singular fit means one or more estimated random-effect variance directions are effectively zero; for example, an intercept–slope covariance matrix can be rank deficient. This may reflect a truly small component or insufficient information, not automatically an optimiser defect. Examine group counts and within-group covariate range, scale predictors, compare defensible simpler structures and fit diagnostics, and consider collecting more independent sites. Thousands of repeated visits do not replace independent sites for estimating between-site variation. Standard errors of variance components and predictions may be asymmetric; profile or parametric bootstrap intervals can be more informative when computationally and statistically feasible. Report boundary fits and sensitivity, not just the model that produced the preferred significance level.

10.4 A Reproducible Simulation and the Salamander Case

The following deliberately small numerical fit uses adaptive one-dimensional integration rather than a production mixed-model package. Eight sites each have twelve visits, with a fixed grid of xx and fixed generating effects; Poisson draws are random. This controlled illustration does not make the eight generated effects a random sample from a normal population. The code maximises the integrated likelihood and compares two numerical integration tolerances. It is educational, not production code: the integration domain used to locate the mode, direct exponentiation and optimisation need stronger safeguards for difficult data.

set.seed(467)
x <- rep(seq(-1.5,1.5,length.out=12),8); group <- rep(1:8,each=12)
b <- rep(c(-.7,-.5,-.3,-.1,.1,.3,.5,.7),each=12)
y <- rpois(length(x), exp(.45+.35*x+b))
d <- data.frame(x,group,y)
pois <- glm(y~x, family=poisson, data=d)
quasi <- glm(y~x, family=quasipoisson, data=d)
nb <- MASS::glm.nb(y~x,data=d)
cat('poisson_quasi_coef_maxdiff',max(abs(coef(pois)-coef(quasi))),
    'quasi_dispersion',summary(quasi)$dispersion,'nb_theta',nb$theta,'\n')
stopifnot(max(abs(coef(pois)-coef(quasi)))<1e-8, summary(quasi)$dispersion>0, nb$theta>0)
gam <- mgcv::gam(y~s(x,k=6),family=poisson,method='REML',data=d)
cat('gam_edf',sum(gam$edf),'prediction',
    predict(gam,newdata=data.frame(x=0),type='response'),'\n')
stopifnot(is.finite(gam$gcv.ubre))
# Marginal random-intercept Poisson likelihood via one-dimensional adaptive integration.
ll_group <- function(par, k, tolerance=1e-7) {
 idx <- group==k; sig <- exp(par[3])
 log_integrand <- function(v)
   sum(dpois(y[idx],exp(par[1]+par[2]*x[idx]+v),log=TRUE))+
   dnorm(v,0,sig,log=TRUE)
 mode <- optimize(function(v) -log_integrand(v),c(-10*sig,10*sig))$minimum
 scale <- log_integrand(mode)
 f <- function(u) exp(vapply(u,log_integrand,numeric(1))-scale)
 scale + log(integrate(f,-Inf,Inf,rel.tol=tolerance)$value)
}
obj <- function(par) -sum(vapply(1:8,function(k) ll_group(par,k),numeric(1)))
fit <- optim(c(coef(pois),log(.4)),obj,method='BFGS',control=list(maxit=300,reltol=1e-9))
cat('glmm_convergence',fit$convergence,'conditional_mu0',exp(fit$par[1]),
    'marginal_mu0',exp(fit$par[1]+exp(2*fit$par[3])/2),
    'sigma',exp(fit$par[3]),'\n')
stopifnot(fit$convergence==0,is.finite(fit$value))
coarse <- sum(vapply(1:8,function(k)ll_group(fit$par,k,1e-5),numeric(1)))
fine <- sum(vapply(1:8,function(k)ll_group(fit$par,k,1e-9),numeric(1)))
cat('glmm_quadrature_loglik_difference',abs(coarse-fine),'\n')
stopifnot(abs(coarse-fine)<1e-5)

The code’s integrated likelihood fits the population coefficients and site variance; it does not yet calculate a prediction for a particular site. The separate held-out calculation linked below evaluates a conditional density for site 1 using that site’s twelve observations and the fitted population distribution. Its grid is a numerical way to average over plausible effects, while the held-out-site score integrates one shared effect over each group of visits.

The executed fit returns β̂0=0.5366\widehat\beta_0=0.5366, β̂1=0.2503\widehat\beta_1=0.2503 and σ̂b=0.4253\widehat\sigma_b=0.4253. At x=0x=0, the fitted zero-effect mean is 1.7101 and the model-based new-site mean is 1.8720. The optimiser reports convergence and the two integration tolerances differ in log likelihood by 4.7×10−114.7\times10^{-11} at the solution. This checks numerical sensitivity at those tolerances, not parameter uncertainty or model adequacy. The site totals are 8, 12, 19, 23, 19, 28, 33 and 42; a common-intercept Poisson fit cannot model their shared site variation. The random-intercept revision allows it, but eight sites leave substantial variance uncertainty. A defensible next check compares simulated site totals and within-site patterns with the observations, and repeats fitting from different starts; if serial patterns remain, revise the within-site model or collect additional independent sites. Do not interpret the convergence code as a diagnostic pass.

Use the fitted eight-site example to distinguish two tasks at x=0x=0. For observed site 1, combine its twelve counts with the fitted normal site distribution and integrate its conditional density on a fine grid. The conditional site-effect mode is −0.615, its mean −0.635, and its central 95% interval −1.132 to −0.176. Integrating this conditional distribution gives expected count 0.934 for a further visit and a simulated central 95% future-count interval 0–3. For a new site, integrate over a fresh normal effect: its population mean is 1.872 and its simulated future-count interval is 0–6. These are different targets; both intervals include count variation, while the observed-site interval also integrates uncertainty in that site’s effect. They condition on fitted fixed effects and variance: uncertainty in those parameters is absent. With just eight sites, a parametric bootstrap or a fully specified posterior would be needed to assess that additional uncertainty, and may itself be unstable.

Now move from a single future count to the joint outcome for a new site. For a new-site check, refit using sites 1–6 only and score the joint vector of the twelve visits at each held-out site 7 and 8. The independent Poisson model’s summed joint log score is −61.935; the integrated random-intercept model’s is −52.123, higher here. The mixed fit estimates a site standard deviation of 0.298 on the training sites. The score integrates a shared random effect across each site’s visits rather than multiplying independent marginal predictions. This one split has only two test sites, and the fixed generating effects in this teaching sample are a deterministic sequence, not independent normal draws; it illustrates prediction and a discrepancy, not reliable validation of the random-effects distribution. Repeat over sites or independent datasets, check integration and convergence, and assess serial, spatial and detection assumptions. A random intercept does not establish that they hold.

The complete reproducible calculation is in examples/extensions-bayes-repairs.R.

For the salamanders, a defensible next model for the GP subset is count ~ mined + DOP + (1 | site), while keeping in mind only 23 sites and four visits each. This model would treat visits as conditionally independent given a site effect; it does not claim independent visits unconditionally. Before interpretation, inspect convergence, variance uncertainty and whether temporal patterns remain, and compare predictions for held-out sites. Mining is a site-level observational exposure, so replication for that association is fundamentally at site level, and a random intercept does not remove ecological confounding or establish causation. This proposal is not a reported salamander mixed-model fit. Recorded counts also conflate occurrence, abundance and detection.

Try it. For the numeric model above, calculate the new-site mean when x=0x=0, then the conditional mean for b=log⁡2b=\log 2. Explain which prediction you would report for a known site with prior visits, a randomly selected new site and a future count at that new site. If each site has only one visit, what evidence distinguishes persistent site heterogeneity from independent count overdispersion?

Outline answer. At x=0x=0 the new-site marginal mean is approximately 1.872, whereas the conditional mean at b=log⁡2b=\log 2 is 2e0.5366≈3.4202e^{0.5366}\approx3.420. For an observed site, integrate its effect conditional on previous visits; for a new site, integrate over the site-effect distribution, and for a future count include count variation as well. With one visit per site, persistent site variation and independent overdispersion can be hard to distinguish without further assumptions or replication.

11 Flexible Effects With Generalised Additive Models

An ecological response need not change at a constant rate along a temperature or elevation gradient. Cutting a continuous gradient into arbitrary low, medium and high categories discards ordering and can produce abrupt fitted jumps; adding many polynomial powers can produce unstable curves at the boundaries. A generalised additive model (GAM) replaces a rigid linear effect with a smooth function while retaining a response distribution, link and interpretable design. Flexibility is controlled by a penalty, and its amount must be estimated or chosen. A smooth is still conditional on the other variables, the sampling design and the response model: a curve alone does not establish a causal optimum.

11.1 Building a Curve From Basis Functions

For a count outcome, consider

Yi∼Poisson⁡(μi),log⁡μi=β0+f(xi)+γzi,f(x)=∑k=1KBk(x)αk. Y_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_i),\quad \log\mu_i=\beta_0+f(x_i)+\gamma z_i,\quad f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}B_k(x)\alpha_k.

Here BkB_k are chosen basis functions and αk\alpha_k their fitted coefficients. The basis converts curve fitting into a regression with columns Bk(xi)B_k(x_i); KK limits the available function space. To see this without specialist software, take B1(x)=xB_1(x)=x, B2(x)=x2B_2(x)=x^2, and coefficients 2 and -1. Then f(0)=0f(0)=0, f(1)=1f(1)=1, f(2)=0f(2)=0. For x=0,1,2x=0,1,2, the basis matrix is

B=(001124),B(2−1)=(010). B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&1\\2&4\end{pmatrix},\qquad B\binom{2}{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}.

These two simple global polynomials explain the construction, not the basis chosen by mgcv::s. Spline bases typically combine locally supported or other smooth functions so a curve can bend in different parts of the observed range. Basis choice and dimension constrain what can be represented even before penalisation. A very small KK cannot express a complex curve; a large enough basis lets the penalty determine how much complexity the data support, subject to computational cost and identifiability.

11.2 Penalising Roughness and Choosing Smoothness

Instead of maximising the log likelihood ℓ\ell alone, estimate coefficients by maximising

ℓ(β,α)−λ2α⊤Sα, \ell(\beta,\alpha)-\frac{\lambda}{2}\alpha^{\top}S\alpha,

where SS is a positive semidefinite penalty matrix and λ≥0\lambda\geq0 determines its strength. For a cubic smoothing spline a common roughness measure is ∫[f″(x)]2dx\int [f''(x)]^2\,dx, which becomes a quadratic form in its basis coefficients. In the simple polynomial example above, on [0,2][0,2], f″(x)=2α2f''(x)=2\alpha_2, so the roughness integral is 8α228\alpha_2^2. At α2=−1\alpha_2=-1 it is 8; doubling the curvature coefficient makes it 32. A large penalty discourages unnecessary curvature. Functions in the penalty’s null space, such as straight lines under a second-derivative penalty, need not shrink to zero as λ\lambda grows.

For this two-column basis, the calculation is explicit: α=(α1,α2)⊤\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)^\top and S=(0008)S=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&8\end{pmatrix}, so α⊤Sα=8α22\alpha^\top S\alpha=8\alpha_2^2. The zero eigenvalue leaves the straight-line direction unpenalised; the other direction is the curvature being charged. Increasing λ\lambda changes how much improvement in likelihood is needed to justify that curvature. It does not by itself tell us which ecological process produced the curve.

The choice of λ\lambda therefore controls a trade-off between following the data and using a smoother curve. A selected value is not an observed ecological quantity: it depends on the basis, likelihood and selection criterion. The effective degrees of freedom (EDF) measure fitted flexibility, not simply the number of basis columns. A roughly straight one-dimensional smooth often has EDF near one after the usual centring constraint; a larger value reflects more flexibility, but is not a count of peaks or a proof that the curve is biologically nonlinear. The smoothing parameter can be selected by criteria including restricted maximum likelihood (REML) or generalised cross-validation (GCV), each with assumptions and possible finite-sample difficulties. For a Gaussian illustration, write the smooth as an unpenalised null-space part X0γX_0\gamma plus a penalised part ZuZu, and take u∼N(0,τ2I)u\sim N(0,\tau^2I) with residual variance σ2\sigma^2. Integrating over uu yields a marginal Gaussian model; REML then forms a likelihood for contrasts that eliminate the fixed coefficients γ\gamma and estimates variance components. Their ratio λ=σ2/τ2\lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2 determines the penalty, after which the coefficient estimates are obtained from the penalised fit. Generalised-response REML uses an approximate marginal criterion, not this exact Gaussian integral. Null-space components and constraints must be treated separately. Estimated smoothness is itself uncertain; ordinary plug-in bands can understate that uncertainty. This representation does not make the ecological sampling design random or correct. The mgcv reference documents smooth construction, selection and diagnostics; Wood (2011) describes stable REML and likelihood-based smoothness estimation.

A truncated-power basis supplies another concrete example of columns used to construct a curve.

An intercept plus an unrestricted smooth can be non-identifiable: adding a constant to ff and subtracting it from the intercept gives the same predictor. Software commonly centres smooths to resolve this. Consequently the plotted smooth is generally a centred partial contribution on the link scale, not the expected count itself. Other covariates and the intercept must be included, followed by the inverse link, to obtain a response prediction. Confidence bands around a fitted smooth represent uncertainty in the estimated effect under the model and software’s approximation; they are not prediction intervals for individual future counts. Pointwise bands also do not simultaneously cover an entire curve with the nominal probability.

11.3 Fit, Inspect and Repair a Simulated Smooth

This example generates a curved mean on a known range. It uses independent Poisson observations and an exposure fixed at one; those assumptions make the demonstration interpretable, not realistic for every survey. Run it in an R environment with mgcv installed. The graph’s vertical axis is the centred link-scale contribution. A rise in the plot means the fitted expected count rises while other terms stay fixed; the vertical zero is imposed by centring, not a no-effect ecological threshold.

set.seed(46710)
n <- 300
x <- runif(n, -2, 2)
z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
eta <- 0.6 + 0.45 * x - 0.30 * x^2 + 0.35 * z
y <- rpois(n, exp(eta))
d <- data.frame(y, x, z)
linear <- glm(y ~ x + z, poisson, data = d)
g <- mgcv::gam(y ~ s(x, k = 10) + z, family = poisson,
               method = "REML", data = d)
summary(g)                   # smooth EDF and approximate uncertainty
plot(g, pages = 1, shade = TRUE, residuals = TRUE)
mgcv::gam.check(g)           # inspect basis check and residual patterns
mgcv::concurvity(g, full = TRUE)
new <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 100), z = 0)
pred <- predict(g, newdata = new, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
new$mean <- exp(pred$fit)
new$lower <- exp(pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
new$upper <- exp(pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
plot(new$x, new$mean, type = "l", ylim = range(new$lower, new$upper),
     xlab = "Gradient", ylab = "Expected count, z = 0")
lines(new$x, new$lower, lty = 2); lines(new$x, new$upper, lty = 2)

In the executed sample the smooth EDF is 3.531 and its basis-check k-index is 1.00. At x≈−0.0202x\approx-0.0202 and z=0z=0, the fitted mean is 1.631 with approximate pointwise interval 1.330–1.999. In four ascending xx bins the linear fit’s mean Pearson residuals are -0.365, 0.166, 0.524, -0.321: the middle is systematically underpredicted and the edges overpredicted. The smooth fit gives -0.038, -0.003, 0.066, -0.045. This is a visible improvement for this generated example, not proof of adequate uncertainty or out-of-sample prediction.

With k=3, EDF is 1.978 of the available 2; increasing to k=10 permits EDF 3.531. The respective k-indices are 0.997 and 0.998, so this particular check does not flag the restricted basis despite its near-saturation. Compare the fitted curves and held-out predictions rather than interpreting one diagnostic as a verdict.

The transformed limits are approximate pointwise intervals for the conditional mean, not for a future observation, and generally do not fully capture every source of smoothing-parameter uncertainty. Compare predictions with the generating mean exp⁡(0.6+0.45x−0.30x2)\exp(0.6+0.45x-0.30x^2) for z = 0; the simulation truth is available here only because we made the data. Check whether the straight-line fit leaves systematic residual curvature. If gam.check suggests the basis dimension is restrictive, refit with a larger k and inspect whether EDF, the curve and held-out performance change. An adequate basis check does not prove the Poisson variance, independence, or curve is correct.

Smooths of strongly related predictors can reproduce one another, a nonlinear analogue of collinearity called concurvity. If w=xw=x exactly, f(x)+g(w)f(x)+g(w) is unchanged when a curve is added to ff and subtracted from gg; the individual contributions are not identified from these data. Near equality makes the problem less obvious. In a separate synthetic example, draw 500 independent gradients xx, make a second measurement w=x+εw=x+\varepsilon with noise standard deviation 0.04, and generate counts from a smooth function of xx. Fit Poisson GAMs to 400 training observations: one has both s(x) and s(w), the other only s(x), each with k=8 and REML smoothing. The two-smooth model’s estimated concurvity measures are 0.9979 for both terms, close to one. Thus the two curves can mimic one another; a precise-looking individual smooth is not a reliable separate ecological attribution.

Suppose the study question and measurement protocol justify retaining xx. The one-smooth repair gives mean held-out log probability −1.61064 per observation versus −1.61100 for two smooths, and their mean absolute difference in predicted counts is 0.0364 on the 100 held-out observations. This check supports retaining the simpler prediction in this sample; it does not prove that ww has no ecological effect. The split holds out one randomly assigned block of independent synthetic observations. It exercises block-level code, but has no spatial or site dependence and is not evidence of spatial generalisation. For genuinely grouped sites, years or spatial blocks, hold out entire relevant groups and repeat across blocks; if the target includes extrapolation, check predictor support. If both predictors are scientifically essential, collect observations that vary them independently or otherwise change the design. Basis size, smoothing choice, prediction uncertainty and alternative data-generating mechanisms remain consequential.

Inspect predictor support jointly, examine concurvity, compare defensible specifications, and avoid attributing separate ecological effects without enough independent variation. Sparse boundary data often yield wider, more assumption-sensitive bands; a smooth can appear deceptively confident outside the sampled range because basis behaviour and penalties determine extrapolation. Plot observations or a rug and report the support. Hold out entire sites, years or spatial blocks if those are the intended units of prediction; a random row split may be too optimistic for new groups.

The complete reproducible calculation is in examples/extensions-bayes-repairs.R.

The fixed-penalty spline calculation is also available in R, Python and Julia. It verifies a shared bounded matrix calculation; it is not a cross-language refit of mgcv’s smoothing-parameter selection.

A GAM can include random effects or correlated error structures, producing a generalised additive mixed model (GAMM). Smoothness penalties and random-effect penalties share a mathematical representation, but a smooth of a predictor and a random site effect represent different scientific components. A flexible mean curve does not remove site dependence; conversely, a random intercept does not correct a misspecified gradient. Fit both only when the design supports their separate estimation, then inspect group-aware residuals and predictions.

Try it. Repeat the simulation using k = 4 and k = 20, holding all other choices fixed. Compare the fitted curve, EDF and diagnostics, then hold out a block of the gradient and predict it. How does this differ from holding out random rows within the observed range? Add a second predictor almost equal to x; what happens to the individual effects and their combined prediction?

Outline answer. Compare the curves, EDF, uncertainty and diagnostics rather than assuming a larger basis is better. Holding out a continuous stretch of the gradient tests interpolation across a gap or extrapolation near an edge, whereas random rows mainly test prediction within observed support. Near-duplicate predictors can make individual curves unstable despite similar combined predictions; the two-smooth example above supplies a concrete check.

12 Zeros, Hurdles and the Observation Process

An observed zero can mean that animals were absent, present but not detected, or present and detected on other occasions but not this one. A Poisson or negative-binomial model already assigns some probability to zero. If the fitted distribution predicts too few zeros, a separate zero component is one candidate, but the discrepancy can also come from rate heterogeneity, omitted covariates or dependence. A zero-inflated model and a hurdle model partition the same observable counts in different ways. Their parameters are useful only relative to their stated generative assumptions; counting zeros alone does not reveal the underlying biology.

12.1 Two Complete Probability Models

Let f(y;μ)f(y;\mu) be any count probability mass function on 0,1,…0,1,\ldots, with mean μ\mu, variance vv, and zero probability f0=f(0;μ)f_0=f(0;\mu). Parameters can vary with covariates and exposure; we suppress subscripts for clarity. A zero-inflated model first assigns probability π\pi to a point-mass zero and otherwise draws from ff:

P(Y=0)=π+(1−π)f0,P(Y=y)=(1−π)f(y;μ),y≥1. P(Y=0)=\pi+(1-\pi)f_0,\qquad P(Y=y)=(1-\pi)f(y;\mu),\quad y\geq1.

Both components can generate an observed zero. For an independent sample, the likelihood is the product of these masses at the observed yiy_i; use the first expression for each zero and the second for each positive count. Its mean and variance follow from the mixture:

E(Y)=(1−π)μ,Var⁡(Y)=(1−π)v+π(1−π)μ2. E(Y)=(1-\pi)\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=(1-\pi)v+\pi(1-\pi)\mu^2.

To derive the variance, condition on the component indicator: the average conditional variance is (1−π)v(1-\pi)v, and the variance of conditional means is π(1−π)μ2\pi(1-\pi)\mu^2. Their sum gives the stated expression. The count-component mean μ\mu is not the overall mean, nor is it generally the mean among positive observations. A logit model for π\pi and a log model for μ\mu produce coefficients with different interpretations. If a predictor appears in both, its overall effect combines both paths; calculate response-scale contrasts instead of interpreting either coefficient alone.

A hurdle model first decides whether the hurdle is crossed, then draws a positive count from the zero-truncated distribution. With q=P(Y>0)q=P(Y>0),

P(Y=0)=1−q,P(Y=y)=qf(y;μ)1−f0,y≥1. P(Y=0)=1-q,\qquad P(Y=y)=q\frac{f(y;\mu)}{1-f_0},\quad y\geq1.

The denominator normalises the positive probabilities: their sum is qq, not q(1−f0)q(1-f_0). The sample likelihood again multiplies the applicable mass for each observation. Its mean and variance are

E(Y)=qμ1−f0,Var⁡(Y)=q(v+μ2)1−f0−(qμ1−f0)2. E(Y)=\frac{q\mu}{1-f_0},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac{q(v+\mu^2)}{1-f_0}- \left(\frac{q\mu}{1-f_0}\right)^2.

Truncation leaves the unnormalised first and second moments unchanged because zero contributes nothing: E(Y∣Y>0)=μ/(1−f0)E(Y\mid Y>0)=\mu/(1-f_0) and E(Y2∣Y>0)=(v+μ2)/(1−f0)E(Y^2\mid Y>0)=(v+\mu^2)/(1-f_0). Multiply both by qq and subtract the squared overall mean to obtain the variance. The parameter μ\mu belongs to the untruncated base distribution; the mean conditional on a positive observation is μ/(1−f0)\mu/(1-f_0). That positive mean exceeds μ\mu whenever f0>0f_0>0. The Stan guide to zero-inflated and hurdle models writes the two likelihoods explicitly.

12.2 A Numerical Comparison and an Identification Surprise

Let the base be Poisson with μ=2\mu=2, so f0=e−2≈0.1353f_0=e^{-2}\approx0.1353. With π=0.25\pi=0.25, the zero-inflated model has zero probability 0.25+0.75e−2≈0.35150.25+0.75e^{-2}\approx0.3515, mean 1.51.5, and variance 0.75(2)+0.25(0.75)(4)=2.250.75(2)+0.25(0.75)(4)=2.25. The conditional mean given a positive count is 2/(1−e−2)≈2.3132/(1-e^{-2})\approx2.313. The point-mass-zero component is not directly observed for any particular zero.

Now use a hurdle model with the same Poisson base and set q=0.75(1−e−2)≈0.6485q=0.75(1-e^{-2})\approx0.6485. Its zero probability is again 0.3515. Its probability of every positive count is also identical:

qf(y;2)1−e−2=0.75f(y;2). q\frac{f(y;2)}{1-e^{-2}}=0.75f(y;2).

Therefore its mean, variance and entire observed count distribution are identical to the preceding zero-inflated model. No analysis of independent counts with this covariate pattern can distinguish these two stories from their probability mass functions. More data improve estimation of that common distribution but do not identify which story generated it. A Poisson hurdle can also represent zero deflation relative to its base by choosing q>1−f0q>1-f_0; a standard zero-inflated model with π≥0\pi\geq0 cannot. For covariates, equivalence requires q(x)=[1−π(x)][1−f0(x)]q(x)=[1-\pi(x)][1-f_0(x)] at every xx. Even when π(x)\pi(x) has a linear logit and μ(x)\mu(x) a linear log, the induced q(x)q(x) generally does not have a linear logit. Consequently the two separately logit-linear regressions in the illustrative package code below need not fit identically. With different regression restrictions, covariates, base families or repeated observations, models may imply distinguishable distributions, but that is a property of the full design and assumptions, not proof of a biological mechanism.

For a different hurdle example, keep μ=2\mu=2 and set q=0.4q=0.4. The probability of zero is 0.6 and the overall mean is 0.4(2)/(1−e−2)≈0.9250.4(2)/(1-e^{-2})\approx0.925. Among positive observations the mean remains about 2.313. By contrast, observing an overall mean of 0.925 does not imply that the mean positive count is 0.925. These quantities answer different questions: probability of any recorded count, expected count given a positive record, and expected count across all records.

12.3 Fitting and Checking Models Without Overclaiming

A practical fit must evaluate log probabilities stably, constrain probabilities and dispersion, and inspect convergence. At a zero, evaluate the log of a sum of component probabilities with stable log-sum-exp arithmetic; at small μ\mu, compute log⁡(1−e−μ)\log(1-e^{-\mu}) using a numerically stable function such as log(-expm1(-mu)). Weak separation of mixture components may give flat likelihoods, extreme coefficients, boundary estimates or singular Hessians. Starting values, multiple plausible initialisations, profile intervals or simulation can expose instability. A numerical optimum is not proof of identification; neither a single zero statistic nor a successful convergence flag establishes the assumed process.

The following bounded intercept-only fit makes the observable calculation explicit. It uses optimised probabilities on transformed scales; it is an educational likelihood, not a production fitting routine. In particular, the simple probability arithmetic can be unstable for extreme parameters.

# Intercept-only mixture and hurdle likelihoods.
set.seed(468); raw <- rpois(300,2); z <- ifelse(runif(300)<.3,0,raw)
zip_obj <- function(par) {pi<-plogis(par[1]); mu<-exp(par[2]);
  -sum(ifelse(z==0,log(pi+(1-pi)*exp(-mu)),
              log1p(-pi)+dpois(z,mu,log=TRUE)))}
hur_obj <- function(par) {q<-plogis(par[1]); mu<-exp(par[2]);
  -sum(ifelse(z==0,log(q),
              log1p(-q)+dpois(z,mu,log=TRUE)-log1p(-exp(-mu))))}
zip <- optim(c(-1,.5),zip_obj,method='BFGS'); hur <- optim(c(-1,.5),hur_obj,method='BFGS')
cat('zi_convergence',zip$convergence,'zero_prob',
    plogis(zip$par[1])+(1-plogis(zip$par[1]))*exp(-exp(zip$par[2])),
    'hurdle_convergence',hur$convergence,'zero_prob',plogis(hur$par[1]),
    'observed_zero',mean(z==0),'\n')
stopifnot(zip$convergence==0,hur$convergence==0)
zip_mean <- (1-plogis(zip$par[1]))*exp(zip$par[2])
hurdle_mean <- (1-plogis(hur$par[1]))*exp(hur$par[2])/
  (1-exp(-exp(hur$par[2])))
cat('zi_mean',zip_mean,'hurdle_mean',hurdle_mean,'observed_mean',mean(z),'\n')
stopifnot(zip_mean>0,hurdle_mean>0)

For the executed sample, 113 of 300 counts are zero (0.3767), the observed mean is 1.4167, and 11 counts are at least 5. The zero-inflated fit gives π̂=0.2731\widehat\pi=0.2731 and μ̂=1.9491\widehat\mu=1.9491, giving fitted zero probability 0.3766 and overall mean 1.4167. The hurdle fit estimates zero probability 0.3767 and base mean 1.9491, giving overall mean 1.4166; this is the same observable fit to numerical tolerance. The fitted zero-inflated model predicts about 10.51 counts at least 5, compared with 11 observed. This single tail comparison does not establish a good fit; simulate the full count distribution and compare several features with uncertainty. An ordinary Poisson model with fitted mean 1.4167 predicts zero probability e−1.4167≈0.2425e^{-1.4167}\approx0.2425, well below the observed 0.3767. The mixture or hurdle revision repairs that discrepancy in-sample, but does not establish the generating mechanism. Both optimisers reported convergence; parameter uncertainty and sensitivity to starting values remain to be assessed.

Refit the same 300 simulated counts after randomly holding out 100. Generate 3,000 test-sized datasets from each training fit. The held-out observations contain 41 zeros, five counts of at least five, and mean 1.53. The ordinary Poisson model predicts central 95% ranges of 17–35 zeros, 0–4 upper-tail counts and means 1.14–1.60. The zero-inflated fit predicts 27–45 zeros, 0–6 upper-tail counts and means 1.10–1.63. The hurdle fit gives 27–45, 0–6 and 1.11–1.63 respectively. Their mean held-out log probabilities are −1.832, −1.687 and −1.687. Thus the two-component revisions address the particular zero and upper-tail discrepancies in this split, without uniquely establishing the mechanism. Their near-identical observable predictions follow from the intercept-only equivalence derived above, not independent confirmation of structural zeros. The ranges condition on fitted parameters, and the single split and chosen summaries leave many possible failures untested. They do not account for site dependence or imperfect detection.

The complete reproducible calculation is in examples/extensions-bayes-repairs.R.

The figure below returns to the equivalence derived above with another set of component probabilities.

The following R code generates a known zero-inflated process and specifies comparable models using glmmTMB. It is illustrative until that package and the code are verified in the chosen runtime. The fits use the same rows and covariates, so their likelihood-based AIC values are comparable as statistical criteria if convergence and likelihood evaluation are sound. The simulation is not evidence that a real species has a structural-zero state.

set.seed(46707)
n <- 600
x <- runif(n, -1, 1)
mu <- exp(0.5 + 0.6 * x)
pi_zero <- plogis(-1 + 0.5 * x)
y <- ifelse(rbinom(n, 1, pi_zero) == 1, 0L, rpois(n, mu))
d <- data.frame(y, x)
pois <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x, family = poisson, data = d)
zi <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x, ziformula = ~ x,
                       family = poisson, data = d)
hurdle <- glmmTMB::glmmTMB(y ~ x, ziformula = ~ x,
                           family = glmmTMB::truncated_poisson(), data = d)
AIC(pois, zi, hurdle)
summary(zi); summary(hurdle)
# Predicted overall mean versus component predictions; check package semantics.
new <- data.frame(x = c(-0.5, 0.5))
predict(zi, newdata = new, type = "response")
predict(zi, newdata = new, type = "conditional")
predict(zi, newdata = new, type = "zprob")

In this package’s hurdle formulation the zero model represents the probability of zero, whereas the notation above uses qq for the probability of a positive observation. Read the package documentation for its prediction types and truncated-family semantics before interpreting them. Generate replicate datasets from each fitted model and compare zero proportions by predictor, the positive-count distribution and its upper tail, not just the total zeros. Compare held-out log scores or other decision-relevant predictions, with site-blocking where observations share sites. If Poisson misses zeros and the hurdle fits, that is evidence about predictive discrepancies under those fitted models, not proof that one ecological process exists. If a model also misses the positive tail, consider a negative-binomial base or omitted group dependence and repeat the checks; extra flexibility must remain supported by data.

12.4 Detection Is a Separate Question

Suppose an animal is present with probability ψ\psi, and conditional on presence is detected on a visit with probability pp. With a single binary observation, P(detection)=ψpP(\text{detection})=\psi p. The combinations (ψ,p)=(0.8,0.5)(\psi,p)=(0.8,0.5) and (0.5,0.8)(0.5,0.8) both give detection probability 0.4: a single detection/non-detection cannot separate occupancy from detection without additional assumptions or information. Counts introduce further complexities, including abundance and repeated detections. A statistical point mass at zero does not automatically estimate absence or detectability. Repeated visits with an explicit observation model, appropriate closure and independence assumptions, or external detection information can help, but require a design and analysis beyond this primer. Even repeated visits cannot rescue assumptions that are scientifically implausible.

For the salamanders, recorded zero counts and repeat visits make an observation-process question plausible; the package data alone and a generic zero-inflated count fit do not establish true absence, true abundance or detection probability. State the estimand as recorded counts, examine site dependence, and describe the missing detection information before assigning a biological label to a zero component.

Try it. With a Poisson base mean 1 and zero-inflation probability 0.3, compute the probability of zero, overall mean and positive-count mean. Construct a hurdle model with the same complete count distribution. Then ask whether a second survey of the same site, with explicitly modelled shared occupancy and visit-specific detection, would add information unavailable in independent one-visit counts; identify the assumptions required.

Outline answer. The zero probability is 0.3+0.7e−1≈0.55750.3+0.7e^{-1}\approx0.5575, the overall mean is 0.70.7, and the mean conditional on a positive count is 1/(1−e−1)≈1.5821/(1-e^{-1})\approx1.582. A hurdle model with zero probability 0.5575 and a zero-truncated Poisson(1) positive part has the same observable distribution. Repeated visits can add information about shared presence and detection, provided closure, the observation model and conditional dependence assumptions are justified.

13 Combining Mean Shape, Site Dependence, and Count Variation

This case brings the preceding modelling decisions together, from specifying a shared-site count model to checking its predictions for sites not used in fitting.

13.1 Model Components and Prediction Targets

The preceding chapters changed one component at a time. A survey can need several changes at once. Suppose site ii has visit jj, recorded positive effort eije_{ij} and gradient xijx_{ij}. A combined model might specify

Yij∣bi∼NB2⁡(μij,κ),log⁡μij=log⁡eij+β0+f(xij)+bi,bi∼N(0,σb2). Y_{ij}\mid b_i\sim\operatorname{NB2}(\mu_{ij},\kappa),\qquad \log\mu_{ij}=\log e_{ij}+\beta_0+f(x_{ij})+b_i,\qquad b_i\sim N(0,\sigma_b^2).

The offset scales the expected recorded count with effort. The smooth changes its mean across the gradient, while bib_i is shared across visits at site ii. Conditional NB2 variation adds observation-level spread μij+μij2/κ\mu_{ij}+\mu_{ij}^2/\kappa even after the shared site effect is specified. A wrong mean can masquerade as either site variation or overdispersion, and few sites or visits may not distinguish the two variance components well. Compare models on the same outcome, covariates and held-out sites; quasi-Poisson alone cannot supply a full count probability for the log score.

To see why the site and NB components answer different questions, write mij=E(Yij∣x,e)=exp⁡(ηij+σb2/2)m_{ij}=E(Y_{ij}\mid x,e)=\exp(\eta_{ij}+\sigma_b^2/2) for the marginal mean, with ηij\eta_{ij} including the offset but not bib_i. If two visits are conditionally independent given their shared bib_i, then for distinct visits j≠kj\ne k,

Cov⁡(Yij,Yik∣x,e)=mijmik{eσb2−1}. \operatorname{Cov}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik}\mid x,e) =m_{ij}m_{ik}\{e^{\sigma_b^2}-1\}.

The covariance comes from the same random multiplier ebie^{b_i} appearing in both conditional means. Independent NB2 variation adds spread to each visit’s conditional distribution but contributes no cross-visit covariance under this conditional-independence assumption. Thus a histogram of individual counts alone cannot separate every source of extra variation; repeated visits give evidence about the shared component. The derivation also assumes the random effect is independent of the covariates and that no additional serial dependence remains.

For an observed site, its prior visits inform its latent effect. For a new site, integrate over a fresh effect rather than treating the fitted effect of an unseen factor as known. If η\eta excludes the random intercept, the zero-effect count mean is eηe^\eta, whereas the new-site marginal mean is eη+σb2/2e^{\eta+\sigma_b^2/2}. To score a whole held-out site’s visits, integrate the product of their conditional NB2 masses over one shared bib_i; multiplying independently marginalised visit probabilities would discard the dependence the model was built to represent. A future-count interval adds outcome and new-site variation; fitted coefficients, dispersion and smoothing parameters bring further uncertainty.

13.2 Simulated Survey and Candidate Models

The next synthetic monitoring programme makes these choices on one common dataset. It is a new case, not the independent NB2 sample or the eight fixed-effect sites above. With seed 4682026, generate 72 independent sites with four visits each. Each visit has a gradient xx uniformly distributed on [−1,1][-1,1] and known positive effort uniformly distributed on [0.6,1.6][0.6,1.6]. The generating site intercept has normal standard deviation 0.55; conditional counts have NB2 shape 2 and mean

μij=eijexp⁡{0.6+0.75sin⁡(πxij)+bi}. \mu_{ij}=e_{ij}\exp\{0.6+0.75\sin(\pi x_{ij})+b_i\}.

Thus the conditional variance is μij+μij2/2\mu_{ij}+\mu_{ij}^2/2. This mechanism is known because we generated it, not because a field survey has confirmed it. Sites 1–54 provide 216 training visits; all four visits from each of sites 55–72 are held out. This split targets a new site, rather than an additional visit at a known one. The same response, covariates and held-out groups are used throughout.

Before inspecting held-out scores, specify five fits: a log-linear Poisson baseline; log-linear NB2; NB2 with a log-linear mean and site intercept; NB2 with a smooth gradient; and NB2 with both smooth and site intercept. The R fit uses mgcv::gam, mgcv::nb(), a seven-dimensional smooth basis, a site random-effect smooth, an effort offset and REML selection. Its NB2 shape and smoothing/site variance parameters are estimated, not fixed at their generating values. The mgcv negative-binomial reference gives the family convention; the random-effects reference explains this penalised representation and its approximations. Non-Gaussian fitting uses an approximate marginal criterion: convergence does not establish identifiability or accurate variance-component uncertainty.

13.3 Training Diagnostics

Before looking at the held-out outcomes, inspect discrepancies on the 54 training sites. Divide the gradient into four fixed bins: [−1,−0.5][-1,-0.5], (−0.5,0](-0.5,0], (0,0.5](0,0.5] and (0.5,1](0.5,1]. Within each bin, average the observed counts minus the model’s marginal expected counts, and sum the four squared bin means. This is a crude summary of a remaining gradient, not a test that can uniquely identify the missing term. Also compare the variance of the 54 site totals, the number of zero counts and the number of counts at least six. The observed values of these last three statistics are 69.24, 62 and 32, respectively.

For each candidate, simulate 1,000 training-sized datasets at the observed training covariates and efforts. For a model with a site term, draw one fresh normal intercept per site and share it across that site’s four visits; draw counts independently conditional on it. The following table gives each observed statistic and the 2.5%–97.5% range of its simulations. These are plug-in checks of marginal site samples with the training design, not simulations conditional on the fitted effects of the observed sites.

Training model Gradient discrepancy: observed; simulated range Site-total variance: observed; range Zeros: observed; range Counts at least six: observed; range
Poisson, linear gradient 4.199; 0.023–0.759 69.24; 13.01–26.95 62; 19–35 32; 16–31
NB2, linear gradient 5.508; 0.130–5.513 69.24; 34.27–121.20 62; 53–79 32; 23–43.03
NB2, linear gradient and site 5.048; 0.119–6.638 69.24; 35.70–178.39 62; 53–80 32; 21–41.03
NB2, smooth gradient 0.147; 0.079–4.046 69.24; 30.19–101.18 62; 53–77 32; 22–41
NB2, smooth gradient and site 0.221; 0.091–4.184 69.24; 32.12–132.52 62; 52–78 32; 20–40

The linear Poisson baseline misses several summaries: its simulated site-total variances and zero counts are below those observed, and its gradient discrepancy is much smaller. That gives a reason to investigate both count variation and mean shape, not a unique diagnosis of either. With the linear NB2 fit, zero and upper-tail counts fall within the simulated ranges, and the site-total variance does too. Its gradient discrepancy, 5.508, lies near the top of its simulated range. In the four ascending bins its mean residuals are −0.197-0.197, −0.076-0.076, 1.4871.487 and −1.803-1.803: the direction of the error changes across the gradient. This pattern motivates considering a smooth mean.

After adding both the smooth and the site term, the corresponding bin means are −0.103-0.103, 0.1730.173, 0.3670.367 and −0.216-0.216, and the squared-bin summary is 0.221. The simulated range for that statistic is 0.091–4.184. These calculations show that the particular training residual pattern is smaller; they do not establish a correct curve or a calibrated predictive distribution. The observed site-total variance was already inside the NB2-only range, so these summaries did not diagnose a site effect. The repeat-visit design and, in this simulation, the known shared generating intercept motivate considering that component; in field data its existence and distribution remain questions for the design and evidence. The NB2 checks also do not establish excess zeros or tails requiring a separate zero process. The zero-process chapter explains why such a component needs a distinct observation model and evidence beyond a count of zeros.

The simulation ranges condition on fitted parameters and do not include refitting or smoothing uncertainty. Their empirical tails use roughly 25 of the 1,000 replicates each, so endpoints have Monte Carlo uncertainty. Several summaries were inspected and they are exploratory; falling inside any one range is not a calibrated goodness-of-fit test or proof of adequacy. The combined example’s complete script records the seeds and the same training design used here.

13.4 Held-Out Comparison and Sensitivity

The table follows the same sites through the modelling decisions. The score is the sum, over 18 held-out sites, of the joint log predictive density of each site’s four visits; larger is better for this realised split.

Training model Estimated NB2 shape Site-effect SD Effective degrees of freedom Held-out joint log score
Poisson, linear gradient Not applicable 0 2.000 −246.089
NB2, linear gradient 1.016 0 2.000 −155.489
NB2, linear gradient and site 1.197 0.366 17.224 −154.160
NB2, smooth gradient 1.208 0 4.956 −155.839
NB2, smooth gradient and site 1.428 0.338 19.326 −152.448

Moving from the Poisson to the linear NB2 model improves this score substantially. Adding a site term gives a smaller further improvement. The smooth without a site term scores slightly worse than linear NB2, while the model containing both has the highest score here. These are differences for one split, not evidence that every component has been identified precisely, or that either smoothness or site variation is always useful. The fitted shape changes between specifications: omitted mean or group structure can be absorbed by a dispersion estimate. Model choice after looking at these scores uses this test set; an independent evaluation or an appropriately nested group-validation procedure would be needed for a fresh estimate of the selected procedure’s performance.

The combined fit also has assumptions about the site variance and the available smooth. gam.vcomp reports a site-effect standard deviation of 0.3383, with approximate interval 0.1618–0.7070; the simulated generating standard deviation was 0.55. This interval reflects an approximate smoothing-parameter calculation, not a definitive test against zero. A variance of zero is a boundary, and a small number of groups can leave this component weakly informed. In this split the no-site smooth candidate’s joint score is −155.839, compared with −152.448 for the combined fit; neither that difference nor the site-total check proves the latent variance.

The basis check for the combined fit gives k-prime 6, smooth EDF 3.942 and k-index 0.940. Its randomisation pp-value is 0.6325 from 400 randomisations, with binomial Monte Carlo standard error approximately 0.024. A non-small value does not prove that the basis is sufficient, and the factor random effect does not have a k-index in this check. As a sensitivity comparison, refit with k=10: the NB2 shape is 1.4319, site SD 0.3404 and total EDF 19.6629, versus 1.4278, 0.3383 and 19.3262 for k=7. The larger-basis score is −152.349 on the same held-out sites, versus −152.448. This reuse is a sensitivity check, not an independent validation set or a warrant to tune the basis on the test outcomes and then call its score untouched evidence.

13.5 Prediction for a New Site

For the first held-out site the four observed counts are (0,0,1,2)(0,0,1,2). Under the combined fit, the four plug-in zero-effect means are (1.25173,1.21587,1.92562,1.04072)(1.25173,1.21587,1.92562,1.04072). If its site effect were known to be b=0.25b=0.25, the conditional means would be (1.60725,1.56120,2.47255,1.33631)(1.60725,1.56120,2.47255,1.33631). A genuinely new site has an unknown effect: integration over its fitted normal distribution gives marginal means (1.32543,1.28746,2.03900,1.10199)(1.32543,1.28746,2.03900,1.10199). The first visit’s integrated predictive probability of zero is 0.409056. These predictions are different because the question changed, not because one is a corrected version of the other.

For one future count with that visit’s covariates and effort, the plug-in new-site predictive interval is 0–6 counts at the 95% equal-tail quantiles. It integrates both a new site effect and conditional count variation. The cumulative probabilities at 5 and 6 are 0.969251 and 0.982517: the upper quantile is the first integer whose cumulative probability reaches 0.975.
