Integer outcomes need not provide exactly 95% coverage between the chosen quantiles. This interval conditions on the fitted model parameters; it does not include uncertainty in the estimated coefficients, smoothing, site variance or NB2 shape.

For all four counts together, the site’s joint log predictive density is −5.200794. To compute it, form the product of the four conditional NB2 probabilities for a candidate site effect, then integrate that product against its normal density. A separate integral for each visit would effectively draw four different site effects and answer a different question. The numerical check compares midpoint quadrature grids and integration ranges; agreement below 10−710^{-7} per site in this case is reassuring for this calculation, not a universal accuracy guarantee. The full predictive distribution is a mixture of NB2 laws, not an NB2 law evaluated at the marginal mean. The numbers integrate new-site heterogeneity but condition on fitted coefficients, shape, smoothing and variance parameters; those extra uncertainty layers are not included.

The full fitted case is in R. Python and Julia reproduce the fixed fitted-input conditional and integrated predictions, future-count interval and joint score using the shared fixture. They do not independently refit the combined model. The synthetic example does not estimate detection, establish a biological zero-generating state, or validate a causal effect. All five fits reported convergence. The checks above expose particular residual, site-total, basis and variance-component questions; neither they nor a single predictive score establish overall adequacy. If a positive tail or zero discrepancy remains after checking those features, consider a different conditional distribution or a zero component with a stated observation model and evaluate it again; neither mechanism follows automatically from one score.

Checkpoint. If a smooth reduces a residual gradient but within-site residual dependence remains, what changed and what remains? The smooth repaired a candidate mean shape; shared-site dependence is a separate claim and needs its own model and group-aware check. A negative-binomial variance can model extra conditional count spread but does not by itself make visits at one site independent after marginalising over a shared site effect.

14 Categorical Responses

A binary response has two possible outcomes; many ecological observations have more. A survey might classify the substrate at a sampled point as rock, sand or vegetation. An assessment might record the condition of a stream reach as poor, moderate or good. These two examples do not have the same structure: substrate categories have no natural order, while condition categories do. In each case the response is one observation in one category, not three independent binary outcomes. The modelling task is to assign probabilities to all possible outcomes jointly, so that the probabilities are non-negative and sum to one. We then ask whether those probabilities change with the explanatory variables and whether the prediction applies to the population and survey design of interest.

14.1 Unordered Categories and the Multinomial Model

Let YiY_i be the category observed for sampling unit ii, let KK be the number of categories, and let pik=P(Yi=k∣𝒙i)p_{ik}=P(Y_i=k\mid\mathbf{x}_i) be the probability of category kk for covariates 𝒙i\mathbf{x}_i. For independent categorical observations, the likelihood is

L(𝜷)=∏i=1n∏k=1KpikI(Yi=k), L(\boldsymbol{\beta})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{k=1}^{K}p_{ik}^{I(Y_i=k)},

where the indicator I(Yi=k)I(Y_i=k) equals one when the observed category is kk and zero otherwise. For grouped counts with a common covariate vector, the corresponding multinomial likelihood includes the multinomial coefficient and raises each category probability to its observed count. That coefficient is constant in the regression parameters when the observations and grouping are fixed, but it matters when comparing likelihood values with other conventions.

A convenient model chooses a reference category, say KK, and sets

log⁡pikpiK=ηik=𝒙i⊤𝜷k,k=1,…,K−1. \log\frac{p_{ik}}{p_{iK}}=\eta_{ik}=\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_k, \qquad k=1,\ldots,K-1.

The K−1K-1 linear predictors describe log probability ratios relative to the reference. Exponentiating and using the fact that probabilities sum to one gives

pik=eηik1+∑j=1K−1eηij,piK=11+∑j=1K−1eηij. p_{ik}=\frac{e^{\eta_{ik}}}{1+\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}e^{\eta_{ij}}}, \qquad p_{iK}=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}e^{\eta_{ij}}}.

This normalisation is often called the softmax. A model that gives every category an unconstrained linear predictor has the same probabilities after adding the same constant to all predictors; without a constraint, the individual coefficient vectors are not identifiable. Setting the reference predictor to zero removes this redundancy. Changing the reference changes the displayed coefficients but not fitted probabilities for the same fitted model. A software implementation may instead impose another identifying constraint, so compare predictions or convert parameterisations before comparing coefficients.

Suppose there are three substrate classes and the reference is vegetation. At a particular covariate value, the log ratios for rock and sand are log⁡2\log 2 and log⁡3\log 3. Their relative weights are therefore 22, 33 and 11, so the fitted probabilities are 1/31/3, 1/21/2 and 1/61/6. Rock is twice as probable as vegetation at this covariate value; it is not automatically twice as probable as sand. If an increase of one unit in a covariate adds log⁡2\log 2 to the rock predictor and leaves the sand predictor unchanged, the weights become 44, 33 and 11. The new rock probability is 1/21/2, sand falls to 3/83/8, and vegetation falls to 1/81/8. The rock-to-vegetation ratio doubles, but the absolute probability changes from 1/31/3 to 1/21/2, not by a fixed amount. The change depends on all category predictors and the starting covariates.

With a fitted model, calculate contrasts in category probabilities for explicit covariate profiles, including uncertainty, instead of treating a coefficient as a probability difference. Interactions and categorical predictors work through the same design-matrix decisions as in binary regression. A category-specific interaction can change the relative association with a gradient; response-scale contrasts remain functions of all categories. The likelihood assumes independent observational units conditional on the model. Multiple observations from one site do not become independent just because their outcomes have several labels.

The multinomial part of examples/extensions.R constructs 240 simulated observations with three unordered labels, fits nnet::multinom, and calculates the probabilities at the centre of the covariate range. In the tested run the probabilities for the factor levels A, B and C were approximately 0.185, 0.345 and 0.469. The numbers add to one up to rounding. The simulation and fit are reproducible from the script’s stated seed; they are one sample, not a proof that the fitted model is correct for an ecological population. The nnet manual describes multinom and its reference-category parameterisation. If a category has very few observations, estimated coefficients may be unstable; separation can cause coefficients to diverge just as in binary logistic regression. Examine category frequencies, convergence and held-out probabilities, and consider a scientifically justified simpler model, regularisation or more data rather than declaring a large coefficient to be a precise effect.

The following is a proposed application, not an executed analysis. A prediction-oriented penguin example poses a different question from modelling body mass as an outcome: given measured features of a bird, how accurately can we predict which of the three observed species was recorded? The Palmer penguins data contain species, island, year and body measurements; their collection and study context are described by Gorman and colleagues and the data authors. Species as an outcome here is a classification exercise. It does not establish that a change in a measurement causes species membership. Nor does accuracy on these sampled birds establish performance on a different population, season or measurement protocol.

Before fitting, decide which predictors would genuinely be available when a future bird is classified. Island can be very predictive while also making the prediction target more restricted; species and island are unevenly represented, so an apparent effect can partly reflect the sampling design. Inspect missing values and report the number excluded, rather than describing complete cases as all sampled birds. Fit preprocessing steps using training data only. Randomly dividing individual birds estimates performance under a different target from holding out a year, field group or island; a split by an appropriate independent unit is needed when prediction for new units is the aim. In particular, do not use a value calculated from the held-out outcomes to construct a training feature. Compare held-out class probabilities and calibration as well as a confusion table; an accurate-looking classifier can still give overconfident probabilities. This is a proposed application, not a claim that such a penguin classification analysis has already been completed.

14.2 Ordered Categories and Thresholds

Now suppose YiY_i takes the ordered values 1,…,K1,\ldots,K, such as poor, moderate and good. An ordinal model can use this ordering without assuming that the difference between poor and moderate has the same numerical meaning as the difference between moderate and good. Define ordered thresholds τ1<⋯<τK−1\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_{K-1} and a linear predictor ηi=𝒙i⊤𝜷\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}. One common cumulative-logit convention is

logit⁡{P(Yi≤k∣𝒙i)}=τk−ηi,k=1,…,K−1. \operatorname{logit}\{P(Y_i\leq k\mid\mathbf{x}_i)\}=\tau_k-\eta_i, \qquad k=1,\ldots,K-1.

Here τk\tau_k describes the baseline cumulative log odds at threshold kk when the non-intercept predictors are zero. The thresholds supply intercepts; including an unconstrained additional intercept in ηi\eta_i would be redundant. Some software writes a plus rather than a minus before the predictor, changing coefficient signs. Interpret a coefficient only after checking the stated convention and category order. With the minus convention above, a positive coefficient shifts probability towards higher categories.

Let F(t)=1/(1+e−t)F(t)=1/(1+e^{-t}). The cumulative probability at threshold kk is F(τk−ηi)F(\tau_k-\eta_i), and an individual category probability is the difference between adjacent cumulative probabilities. For example, for three ordered categories, P(Yi=1)=F(τ1−ηi)P(Y_i=1)=F(\tau_1-\eta_i), P(Yi=2)=F(τ2−ηi)−F(τ1−ηi)P(Y_i=2)=F(\tau_2-\eta_i)-F(\tau_1-\eta_i) and P(Yi=3)=1−F(τ2−ηi)P(Y_i=3)=1-F(\tau_2-\eta_i). Ordering the thresholds ensures that these probabilities are non-negative.

Take τ1=−1\tau_1=-1, τ2=1\tau_2=1 and first set ηi=0\eta_i=0. The cumulative probabilities are about 0.269 and 0.731, so the category probabilities are approximately (0.269,0.462,0.269)(0.269,0.462,0.269). At ηi=1\eta_i=1 the cumulative probabilities become about 0.119 and 0.500; the category probabilities become (0.119,0.381,0.500)(0.119,0.381,0.500). The model puts more probability on the highest outcome, although the change in the middle category is not described by a single odds ratio. For a one-unit increase in a predictor whose coefficient is one, the odds of being at or below either threshold are multiplied by e−1e^{-1}. Equivalently, the odds of being above either threshold are multiplied by ee. That common multiplier is the proportional-odds assumption; it concerns cumulative odds, not equal category probabilities or equal numerical distances between labels. McCullagh’s original ordinal regression paper develops this family of models.

In examples/extensions.R, a simulated continuous latent score plus logistic noise is cut at two thresholds to create three ordered categories. A logistic MASS::polr fit gives, at x=0x=0, probabilities approximately (0.299,0.394,0.307)(0.299,0.394,0.307) for low, medium and high. These values are a reproducible fit to that generated sample, rather than evidence about real stream condition. The following R fragment reproduces the ordered fit; the complete executable script also contains the multinomial and remaining examples.

R:

set.seed(469)
N <- 240
x <- seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = N)
latent <- rlogis(N) + 0.7 * x
condition <- ordered(cut(latent, c(-Inf, -0.7, 0.7, Inf),
                         labels = c("low", "medium", "high")))
fit <- MASS::polr(condition ~ x, Hess = TRUE, method = "logistic")
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = 0), type = "probs")

The MASS polr documentation describes the ordered response and sign convention. Compare predicted probabilities at several covariate values, not only at the centre, and show uncertainty when interpreting fitted differences.

The proportional-odds restriction can be wrong. For example, restoration might make severely degraded reaches less common without changing the distinction between moderate and good reaches to the same degree. Compare observed and predicted cumulative probabilities across relevant covariate ranges, inspect threshold-specific binary fits as an exploratory diagnostic, and assess a less restrictive model with an appropriate test or validation strategy. The separate binary fits are correlated and can produce crossing cumulative probabilities; they are diagnostic comparisons, not automatically a coherent replacement. A partial proportional-odds model can allow selected slopes to vary by threshold while preserving ordered predicted cumulative probabilities in the intended range; a multinomial model is another option that gives up the ordering constraint and uses more parameters. Check that the data support the added flexibility and assess category probability calibration on held-out units.

The executable case examples/ordinal-repair.R makes that decision concrete. It simulates 3,000 independent observations with xx uniformly distributed from −1-1 to 11. The lower cumulative logit is −1−0.2x-1-0.2x and the upper is 1−1.1x1-1.1x. The cumulative probabilities remain ordered throughout this interval, but the two slopes are deliberately different. Fit both separate binary cumulative logits to the first 2,000 observations as a diagnostic: the observed slopes in this run are about −0.128-0.128 and −1.241-1.241. The proportional-odds model estimates one shared cumulative-logit slope, about −0.684-0.684 in this convention. The fitted diagnostic slopes need not equal their generating values exactly, but their difference reveals what the single shared slope is being asked to compress.

We pre-specify a multinomial model as the less restrictive alternative and evaluate both fitted models on the same remaining 1,000 observations. Lower is better for both scores: held-out mean log loss is 1.045 for proportional odds and 1.031 for multinomial; the multicategory Brier scores are 0.631 and 0.621. At x=0.8x=0.8, for example, the true generating probabilities are approximately (0.239,0.291,0.470)(0.239,0.291,0.470); proportional odds predicts (0.157,0.437,0.406)(0.157,0.437,0.406) and multinomial predicts (0.225,0.286,0.489)(0.225,0.286,0.489). This is a comparison of probabilities for the same categories, not an estimate of one shared ordinal odds ratio from the multinomial fit. The multinomial alternative uses more parameters and gives up the proportional-odds ordering structure; its better score in this deliberately selected simulation is not a guarantee in another sample. A real analysis should state candidate models and validation design before comparing them, and report uncertainty in predictive performance rather than selecting a model by repeatedly searching the test set.

The grouped-binomial likelihood and the Poisson count likelihood are still the same sampling models when we change inferential approach. The next step adds a prior to each, then separates uncertainty in parameters from variation in a future observation.

15 Bayesian Models

A likelihood describes how the observations would vary for a specified parameter value. In Bayesian inference we combine that same sampling model with a probability distribution for the parameters before observing the current data. The resulting posterior distribution describes uncertainty about the parameters conditional on the model, prior and observed data. This does not remove the need to check sampling design, likelihood assumptions or computation. It adds an explicit question: which parameter values and observable outcomes were plausible before these data, and how much did the data change that judgement?

15.1 Updating a Probability: Likelihood, Prior and Posterior

Let YY be the number of observed detections in nn independent visits with the same detection probability pp. Conditional on pp, take Y∼Binomial⁡(n,p)Y\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p). This is a model for observed detections under the stated assumptions, not a model that establishes true occupancy. With observed value yy, the likelihood as a function of pp is proportional to py(1−p)n−yp^y(1-p)^{n-y}. Suppose the prior is p∼Beta⁡(a,b)p\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b), with a>0a>0 and b>0b>0. Multiplying the likelihood by the prior density gives

π(p∣y)∝pa+y−1(1−p)b+n−y−1. \pi(p\mid y)\propto p^{a+y-1}(1-p)^{b+n-y-1}.

The normalised posterior is therefore Beta⁡(a+y,b+n−y)\operatorname{Beta}(a+y,b+n-y). The proportionality constant can be found by integrating the product over 0<p<10<p<1; in this example recognition of the beta density supplies it. This is called a conjugate update because the prior and posterior belong to the same distribution family. Conjugacy is a useful calculation, not a requirement of Bayesian modelling.

With a Beta⁡(2,2)\operatorname{Beta}(2,2) prior and seven detections in ten visits, the posterior is Beta⁡(9,5)\operatorname{Beta}(9,5), with mean 9/14≈0.6439/14\approx0.643. The data-only sample proportion is 0.7 and the prior mean is 0.5. The posterior mean lies between them because both the prior and the likelihood contribute. The script examples/extensions.R evaluates this mean both from the beta formula and by numerical integration; their difference in the tested run was about 1.1×10−161.1\times10^{-16}. That check verifies this calculation, not the equal-probability or independence assumptions about actual visits.

The next figure gives a separate conjugate update with two successes and eight failures.

This second calculation deliberately changes the observed data: the same Beta(2,2) prior becomes Beta(4,10), not Beta(9,5). Comparing the two updates shows how the direction of the likelihood shifts a common prior; neither figure is the outcome of both datasets at once.

A posterior credible interval for pp is an interval containing a stated fraction of the posterior probability under the prior and likelihood. It is conditional on the model and observed data. A frequentist confidence-interval procedure is instead assessed by its coverage over repeated datasets under its assumptions; its nominal coverage does not mean that, after the data are fixed, the unknown fixed parameter has that probability of lying in the computed interval. Both approaches can be useful, but their probability statements answer different questions. A credible interval’s probability statement is not a guarantee that the sampling design was representative or that the prior was appropriate.

The posterior mean is not the complete answer if the next question concerns future counts. For mm future visits, draw pp from the posterior and then draw a future count from Binomial⁡(m,p)\operatorname{Binomial}(m,p). Repeating both steps gives the posterior predictive distribution. The first step propagates uncertainty about pp; the second includes variation in future observations even if pp were known. In this particular beta-binomial example the predicted number in mm visits has mean m(a+y)/(a+b+n)m(a+y)/(a+b+n). For one further visit, the predictive detection probability is 9/149/14; a future 0 or 1 remains uncertain even if the posterior for pp becomes very concentrated. If future visits differ in weather, observer or site, the single common-probability model does not account for those differences.

15.2 Count-Model Updating and Predictive Checks

Consider twelve hypothetical independent equal-effort surveys with recorded counts 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9: total 28. For a first model, Yi∣λ∼Poisson⁡(λ)Y_i\mid\lambda\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda) with a shared rate, and λ∼Gamma⁡(2,1)\lambda\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2,1) using shape and rate. The prior mean is two counts per survey. Multiplying likelihood and prior gives λ∣y∼Gamma⁡(2+28,1+12)=Gamma⁡(30,13)\lambda\mid y\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(2+28,1+12)=\operatorname{Gamma}(30,13). Its mean is 2.308 and central 95% credible interval is 1.557–3.204 counts per survey.

The frequentist Poisson maximum-likelihood rate is 28/12 = 2.333. The two estimates are close here, but the credible interval is conditional on the specified prior and model; it is not a frequentist confidence interval.

A future count varies even if the rate were known. Integrating its Poisson distribution over the posterior yields a negative binomial with size 30 and success probability 13/1413/14 in R’s parameterisation. Its central 95% integer predictive interval is 0–6 counts, wider in purpose than the interval for the mean rate.

A stronger Gamma(10,5) prior has the same prior mean but yields posterior mean 2.235; compare intervals and predictions under scientifically plausible alternatives, rather than calling a prior automatically non-informative.

Predictive checking can challenge assumptions before and after the data. Had we initially used Gamma(2,10), whose prior mean is 0.2, 30,000 prior predictive datasets of twelve surveys have a central 95% total-count range 0–8. That clashes with the 28 counts observed here; it also prompts a pre-data question about whether totals that low were plausible for the intended monitoring programme. We instead examine Gamma(2,1), whose prior predictive total range is 2–69. This is a sensitivity demonstration, not a rule that priors should be tuned until observed data fit.

Under Gamma(2,1), posterior predictive replicated datasets have 0–4 zeros in their central 95% range, compared with seven observed.

The common-rate Poisson model misses that feature. One stated repair allows each survey its own independent Gamma-distributed rate with mean λ\lambda and fixed shape one. Integrating the rate gives NB2 counts with mean λ\lambda and variance λ+λ2\lambda+\lambda^2; keep the Gamma(2,1) prior for λ\lambda and evaluate its one-dimensional posterior on a fine grid. Its posterior mean is 2.379, and its simulated posterior predictive zero range is 1–7; the corresponding tail-at-least-five range is 0–6 versus three observed. The revised check is compatible with these summaries, not proof that individual rates really are Gamma distributed. Fixed shape one is an illustrative assumption, not an estimated dispersion; assess shape and prior sensitivity, and collect replication to distinguish heterogeneity, dependence and detection. Checks use the same data twice and their central ranges are descriptive, not calibrated hypothesis tests.

The complete reproducible calculation is in examples/extensions-bayes-repairs.R. The repaired-model posterior mean changes by 2.12×10−72.12\times10^{-7} when the grid extends to 20; the wider grid assigns about 1.09×10−71.09\times10^{-7} probability above 11. This checks truncation for this target, not the fixed-shape assumption.

For the original common-rate calculation, the total 28 is the sufficient count entering the Gamma update, together with the twelve equal exposures. The posterior interval concerns the unknown common rate. To predict a future count, first draw a rate from that posterior and then a Poisson observation given that rate; the second draw adds variability that an interval for the rate alone cannot contain. The separate NB repair changes the sampling distribution, not merely the width of the original interval. The analytic count calculation also has Python and Julia implementations; these check the stated conjugate target rather than the full hierarchical sampler.

15.3 Priors and a Logistic Regression

For binary observation YiY_i, use Yi∼Bernoulli⁡(pi)Y_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i) and logit⁡(pi)=𝒙i⊤𝜷\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}. A Bayesian model supplies a joint prior for the regression coefficients 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta}. For example, after centring and scaling a continuous covariate, one might use independent normal priors with mean zero and a declared standard deviation on the intercept and slope. These are distributions on the log-odds scale: an apparently modest slope can imply a large odds ratio over the full observed covariate range. An intercept prior describes the probability at the predictor’s reference value, not the overall prevalence unless the reference and target population make that interpretation appropriate.

Choose prior scales in the units actually used in the model. Before seeing the response values, draw coefficients from the proposed prior, transform through the inverse logit for plausible covariate profiles, and simulate observations. If ordinary-looking coefficient draws put almost every site at probabilities near zero or one, reconsider the scale or explain why such extremes are plausible. A prior predictive check can also expose implausible counts or combinations of categories. It does not use the observed outcome to estimate the posterior, although the domain, design and genuinely prior information must still be specified. When a prior is informed by earlier data, state the source and whether those data are independent of the present likelihood.

Separation shows why the prior is not cosmetic. Suppose every detection occurs at a positive covariate value and every non-detection at a negative value. An unpenalised logistic likelihood can approach its supremum while the slope tends to infinity; there is no finite maximum-likelihood slope in this simple separated case. A proper normal prior downweights arbitrarily large coefficients and yields a proper posterior for this bounded Bernoulli likelihood. The resulting finite estimate is not data alone: the strength and tails of the prior affect the answer, potentially substantially. Compare at least two defensible prior scales and report how the predicted probabilities and conclusions change. In the ten-observation case below, independent zero-centred normal priors with standard deviations 1, 2 and 3 on both intercept and slope give posterior predictive probabilities at x=1x=1 of about 0.582, 0.593 and 0.595, respectively. These are sensitivity calculations for one prediction, not proof that all posterior features are insensitive.

The calculation expands the grid from [−6,6][-6,6] to [−8,8][-8,8] for the widest prior and obtains a difference below 10−810^{-8} for this prediction; wider tails or another summary can still require a different range. If the data do not distinguish plausible prior choices, that sensitivity is part of the result rather than a computational defect to hide. A prior cannot correct confounding, unrepresentative sampling or an unmodelled detection process merely by stabilising a fit.

For the ten simulated observations in examples/bayes.R, both the intercept and slope have independent N(0,22)N(0,2^2) priors. The script evaluates the unnormalised posterior on a two-dimensional grid from −6-6 to 66 and normalises the values. The tested grid gives posterior mean intercept about −0.120-0.120, mean slope 0.5540.554, and posterior predictive detection probability about 0.593 at x=1x=1. A separate script compares grids with 161 and 321 points per dimension and checks posterior mass near the boundary. Grid agreement in this example supports the numerical approximation over the examined range; it does not establish that an arbitrary grid in a larger model captures every important region. In particular, refine spacing and expand the range when the posterior is narrow, heavy-tailed or close to a boundary.

15.4 From a Grid to Markov Chain Monte Carlo

A grid with two coefficients is manageable. With twenty coefficients, evaluating even a modest number of points per dimension becomes impractical because the number of grid cells grows exponentially. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) instead constructs a sequence whose long-run distribution is the posterior under suitable conditions. It need not visit each point independently. Its attraction is that it can explore a high-dimensional posterior without enumerating a complete grid; its difficulty is that correlated draws and inadequate exploration can produce apparently precise but unreliable summaries.

In random-walk Metropolis, start at a coefficient vector 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} and propose a nearby vector 𝜷′\boldsymbol{\beta}' from a symmetric proposal distribution. Evaluate the unnormalised posterior density at both. Accept the proposal with probability

min⁡{1,π(𝜷′∣𝒚)π(𝜷∣𝒚)}; \min\left\{1,\frac{\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}'\mid\mathbf{y})}{\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}\mid\mathbf{y})}\right\};

otherwise retain the current vector. The unknown posterior normalising constant cancels. In an implementation, calculate the log-density difference to reduce underflow. An asymmetric proposal needs the corresponding forward and reverse proposal-density ratio. Rejection is a repeated state, not an observation to discard: keeping repetitions is part of the chain’s distribution. Small proposal steps may have high acceptance but move slowly; very large steps may be rejected often. Neither extreme nor an acceptable-looking acceptance rate proves that the chain has explored all important regions.

The accompanying examples/bayes.R starts four chains from dispersed locations for the simulated two-coefficient logistic model, discards the first 5,000 iterations of each as a simple warm-up and keeps 25,000 per chain. In the tested run the pooled posterior mean intercept was −0.112-0.112, the mean slope 0.5530.553, and the predictive probability at x=1x=1 was 0.594. These are close to the grid’s −0.120-0.120, 0.554 and 0.593, respectively. Acceptance was about 0.48 per chain, and lag-one autocorrelation for the intercept was about 0.83. This substantial autocorrelation means that 100,000 retained states do not contain the same information as 100,000 independent posterior draws. The grid is an independent numerical benchmark for this small target.

For the predictive probability, the script divides each retained chain into 50 consecutive batches of 500, estimates each chain mean variance from its batch means, and combines the four independent chain variances. This gives an estimated Monte Carlo standard error of 0.00169 for the pooled mean; its difference from the grid value is 0.00154. Batch-means accuracy depends on chains having reached stationarity, sufficiently long batches and reliable variance estimation; the comparison is evidence for this particular scalar calculation, not a general convergence guarantee.

Multiple chains and trace plots can expose failures that one chain hides. Compare chains started in dispersed plausible regions and inspect movement, stability and whether they visit similar regions. A conventional split-R̂\widehat{R} compares between-chain and within-chain variation after splitting chains; values noticeably above one indicate disagreement. Modern implementations also use rank normalisation and folding, which help reveal scale and tail problems that the classical statistic can miss. Bulk and tail effective sample sizes concern different summaries of the distribution. For an ideal stationary scalar sequence with NN draws and lag-tt autocorrelation ρt\rho_t, the conceptual relationship is

Neff≈N1+2∑t=1∞ρt. N_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t}.

Estimating the infinite sum from finite, possibly nonstationary chains needs care; the formula is not an instruction to sum a noisy sample autocorrelation indefinitely. Effective sample size is summary-dependent, and Monte Carlo standard error depends on it and the quantity being estimated. See Vehtari and colleagues’ improved diagnostics and the Stan effective sample size discussion. The example records acceptance and a lag-one correlation but does not implement or report vetted general-purpose R̂\widehat{R}, effective sample size or Monte Carlo standard errors; its reported batch-means Monte Carlo standard error is a narrow estimate under the stated assumptions. Before using a posterior for a substantive result, use a tested diagnostics implementation, investigate warnings and report the uncertainty of the Monte Carlo estimate when it matters. Passing diagnostics does not establish that the ecological model or prior is correct.

Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) uses gradients and auxiliary momentum to propose more distant moves while approximately following trajectories through the posterior; a numerical integrator and a Metropolis correction account for discretisation. The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) adapts trajectory length rather than requiring one fixed path length. These methods can explore some continuous multivariate posteriors much more efficiently than a simple random walk, but difficult geometry, poor scaling, divergences or poorly identified parameters can still make draws unreliable. Reparameterisation, more informative justified priors, a better design or a simpler model may help; merely increasing iterations is not a general cure. See the original NUTS paper and Stan’s discussion of divergences. The small grid and random-walk scripts are teaching devices, not an HMC/NUTS implementation. A larger hierarchical or mixture analysis should use an independently tested dedicated sampler, documented model code, diagnostics and reproducible runtime rather than silently scaling up the toy algorithm.

15.5 Checking Posterior Predictions

Posterior predictive checking asks whether data simulated from the fitted model resemble the observations in features relevant to the question. For each posterior draw, calculate probabilities for the observed covariates and simulate a new response dataset. Compare, for example, the number of detections, detection rates across a gradient, and site-to-site variation with the observed quantities. If simulated datasets consistently have less between-site variation than the observations, a common-probability independent-visit model may be missing heterogeneity or dependence. That pattern does not by itself identify the correct repair: site effects, varying effort or an observation process may lead to similar discrepancies. State a plausible revision and check it again. Posterior predictive agreement is useful evidence against particular detectable failures, not proof of the model’s truth.

The same ten-observation logistic case provides a small numerical check. With the N(0,22)N(0,2^2) coefficient priors and the observed predictor values held fixed, 30,000 prior-predictive datasets have all ten outcomes equal to zero or all equal to one about 9.9% of the time. That is a statement about this proposed prior, design and statistic; whether it is implausible depends on domain knowledge and sampling context. It is not the observed frequency of extreme field datasets.

For posterior prediction, examples/bayes.R samples coefficient pairs from the normalised grid, then draws new binary outcomes at the same ten predictors. The observed dataset has five detections. About 0.610 of simulated datasets have at least five; this is an upper-tail fraction with ties included. As a second preselected discrepancy, subtract the number of detections at negative xx from the number at positive xx, excluding the observation at zero. The observed difference is two; about 0.624 of simulated datasets have an absolute difference of at least two. Both fractions have Monte Carlo variation, depend on the fitted prior and model, and use data twice in the posterior predictive comparison. They are not uniformly distributed frequentist pp-values, and neither value establishes adequacy. Inspect the simulated distributions and discrepancies relevant to the scientific question. If a check suggested a missing group effect or an implausible gradient, propose a model that addresses that specific mismatch and rerun the check; do not choose the most favourable statistic after looking at many alternatives.

15.6 Hierarchical Sharing Across Sites

This next hierarchy revisits the partial-pooling idea from the mixed-model chapter. Here the site-specific latent quantity is a probability with a beta distribution, rather than the normal log-rate intercept in the count GLMM. Both share information across sites, but their likelihoods and response-scale interpretations are different.

A hierarchical model formalises one way to share information between sites while allowing real differences. Consider four sites, each with ten comparable visits, and observed detection counts (1,4,7,9)(1,4,7,9). Let pjp_j be the detection probability for site jj. For this deliberately narrow example, let the shared mean mm have prior Beta⁡(2,2)\operatorname{Beta}(2,2) and let

pj∣m∼Beta⁡(6m,6(1−m)),Yj∣pj∼Binomial⁡(10,pj). p_j\mid m\sim\operatorname{Beta}(6m,6(1-m)), \qquad Y_j\mid p_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(10,p_j).

The positive number 6 fixes the prior concentration: larger values would pull site probabilities more strongly towards mm before observing the site outcomes. It is fixed here, not estimated from the four sites. The conditional posterior of each site probability given mm and its data is

pj∣m,Yj=yj∼Beta⁡(6m+yj,6(1−m)+10−yj). p_j\mid m,Y_j=y_j\sim\operatorname{Beta}(6m+y_j,6(1-m)+10-y_j).

We still have uncertainty about mm. Integrating out the site probabilities gives a beta-binomial marginal likelihood for mm, which can be multiplied by the prior and evaluated on a one-dimensional grid. The script examples/bayes.R normalises that grid, samples a value of mm from it and then samples each pjp_j from its exact conditional beta distribution. Its numerical posterior site means are approximately (0.258,0.445,0.633,0.758)(0.258,0.445,0.633,0.758), compared with raw proportions (0.1,0.4,0.7,0.9)(0.1,0.4,0.7,0.9). Repeated conditional samples give means within 0.001 of the grid calculation in the tested run. Extreme site estimates move towards the shared distribution: this is partial pooling, not an assertion that every site has the same probability. Sites with fewer observations would generally be influenced more by the common distribution, holding other features fixed.

This simple hierarchy also makes its limitations visible. The chosen concentration and hyperprior are assumptions; repeat the analysis with defensible alternatives. The beta distribution assumes a particular form for variation across sites, and the binomial layer assumes comparable independent visits conditional on each pjp_j. A site probability of detection is not occupancy, and if the sampling process omits inaccessible sites, pooling cannot recover a representative regional average by itself. More elaborate Bayesian GLMMs can put a distribution on a random-intercept scale, estimate its spread and include site covariates, but require checks for weakly identified variance components and careful prediction for new groups. The hierarchy above demonstrates the mechanism and a numerically tractable check; it is not a generic sampler for those models.

The following comparison shows the four-site partial-pooling calculation just described.

16 Model-Building Synthesis

A useful analysis is a sequence of decisions linked to an ecological question, not a contest in which the most elaborate model wins. The sequence can loop back: a diagnostic may show that the sampling description or response definition needs revision before a different likelihood is worth fitting.

The combined survey gives this sequence a specific outcome. On the 54 training sites, the linear Poisson model underpredicted the observed site-total variation and zeros, while the linear NB2 model’s bin residuals still changed from 1.487 to −1.803 across the last two gradient bins. The combined smooth-and-site fit reduced those bin residuals to 0.367 and −0.216. The observed site-total variance also lay inside the NB2-only range, so it did not diagnose a shared site effect: the repeat-visit design motivates examining that component, and the simulation’s generating effect is known only by construction.

All five candidate fits were evaluated on the same 18 held-out sites. The Poisson-to-NB2 score change favoured the NB2 distribution in this split; the combined model scored highest, although the smooth without a site effect did not improve on linear NB2. The basis-size comparison reused those sites and is sensitivity evidence, not another validation sample. The site-55 predictions then distinguished a zero-effect site, a hypothetical known effect and a new-site average. These results support a prediction comparison for this simulation, not a conclusion that the generating components have been uniquely recovered. The training simulation ranges omit parameter uncertainty, and further design-matched checks and independent sites remain valuable after selection.

The real Salamanders case answers a more limited question. Its 92 GP visit records support the stated recorded-count association with mining and scaled precipitation, but the row split and held-site split assess different future units. The NB2 fit changes the variation model while leaving repeated sites untreated; the proposed random-intercept revision is not a reported real fit. Neither the synthetic result nor a fitted count model determines how many animals were present but missed. A detection protocol and a design that separates occurrence from observation are required for that additional question.

First state what was sampled, what was observed and what population or future units the answer concerns. For repeated salamander visits, a recorded count or a positive count is an observed outcome at a visit. Whether a species was present but missed is a separate observation-process question. Identify site, visit, species and any exposure actually recorded; do not invent an effort offset. For penguin measurements, state the variables used, missingness and the sampled birds to which the comparison applies. A conditional association between species and mass is not automatically an effect of changing species.

Next choose a response distribution and a link that reflect the response support and the proposed mean–variance relationship. Write the design matrix explicitly enough to identify reference levels, interactions and constraints. Define offsets in units and ask whether their coefficient really should be fixed at one. For an ordinal response, the cumulative odds are a modelling assumption; for overdispersed counts, quasi-likelihood and negative binomial fitting answer overlapping but not identical questions. A quasi model specifies estimating relationships without supplying an ordinary full likelihood for AIC or a complete predictive distribution.

Fit a transparent baseline, inspect convergence, rank and separation, and translate coefficients into the contrasts or predictions that answer the question. Compare uncertainty about a mean with variability of a future observation. For nonlinear links, averaging transformed predictions is generally different from transforming an averaged linear predictor. If groups are present, specify whether the target is conditional on an observed group or marginal over new groups; those estimands can differ. Make the covariate values, population and exposure used for every reported prediction explicit.

Then compare the fitted model with evidence that could contradict it. Residual and simulation checks, calibration, influential observations, dispersion and group-aware or time-aware validation each reveal different kinds of failure. Select a validation split matching the intended prediction task; putting repeated observations from the same site in both training and test sets can make new-site performance look too optimistic. If the model fails, connect the repair to a credible mechanism or changed assumption, fit it, and repeat the relevant comparison. A negative-binomial variance can address one form of extra count variation; it does not automatically remove temporal dependence or identify why excess zeros occurred. A zero-inflated fit may match a zero count without proving a latent biological class.

Finally communicate the answer on the original response scale with units, interval type, sampling population and limitations. Separate decisions made before looking at the data from decisions made after inspecting diagnostics. Present plausible alternative models or prior sensitivities when they change the result. If the design cannot answer the question, say so and specify what additional measurements or sampling would make progress possible. A numerical estimate with a narrow model-based interval is not a substitute for an identifiable target.

17 Further Study and Boundaries

The methods in this primer cover a useful range, but several common ecological questions change the response model, the observation process or the dependence structure. Recognising the boundary is an analytical result: it prevents a convenient model from being asked to answer a question it cannot identify.

  • Continuous proportions: A count of successes out of a known number of trials has a binomial denominator. A continuous fraction measured between zero and one, such as estimated cover, has a different measurement process; beta regression may be useful for values strictly inside that interval. Exact zeros and ones need additional modelling choices, and estimated cover may have measurement error. See the original beta-regression treatment by Ferrari and Cribari-Neto. Do not replace a count denominator with a beta model merely because the response was written as a proportion.
  • Zero plus positive continuous values: A response such as biomass can combine exact zeros with a continuous positive distribution. A two-part model can separately describe occurrence and positive amount; some compound Poisson–Gamma Tweedie distributions provide another model under particular power parameters. The choice changes the scientific and statistical assumptions. See Tweedie GLM documentation for the variance-power family and limits; model fit alone cannot identify the ecological source of zeros.
  • Imperfect detection and occupancy: Repeated non-detections do not prove absence. Occupancy models distinguish a latent presence process from detection conditional on presence and depend on repeat-visit and closure assumptions. See MacKenzie and colleagues. If visits are dependent, species identification is uncertain or occupancy changes during sampling, the basic model may not answer the intended question without further work.
  • Spatial and temporal dependence: A site random intercept can represent shared variation within a group but does not automatically capture spatial correlation between neighbouring sites or serial correlation across time. Map residuals, inspect their temporal structure and define the target of prediction. Spatially or temporally structured models and blocked validation may be necessary; see the INLA latent Gaussian modelling paper for one principled modelling framework. A spatial term cannot by itself establish causality or eliminate unmeasured spatial confounding.
  • Time to an event: If observation ends before an event occurs, the censored duration contains information different from an ordinary count or binary outcome. Survival models represent event times and censoring directly; see Cox’s proportional-hazards paper. Decide whether the censoring and risk-set assumptions fit the study before applying the method.

For the main routes, return to Nelder and Wedderburn’s GLM paper for the original common fitting framework, and to the R glm documentation for the implementation used here. McCullagh’s ordinal models develop the ordered-response route; Vehtari and colleagues explain improved MCMC diagnostics. These sources are starting points for the stated problems, not substitutes for checking the sampling design and assumptions of a particular analysis.

18 Exercises and Outline Solutions

The exercises revisit calculations, assumptions, interpretation and model revision. Use the outline answers to check the reasoning; simulated outputs may vary when you change a seed or generating mechanism.

18.1 Foundations and Core Models

These exercises use hypothetical values unless a dataset is named. Work on the stated scale first, then explain what your answer says about an observation and what it cannot establish.

  1. A Gaussian model has mean 12+2x+3h−xh12+2x+3h-xh, where hh is one for restored habitat. Calculate both habitat means at x=2x=2 and the restored-minus-reference contrast. Explain the intercept.
  2. A logistic model has baseline probability 0.25 and an odds ratio of three. Calculate the new odds and probability. Is the probability three times as large?
  3. Two visits last one and four hours. A fitted rate is 0.8 observations per hour at both visits. Calculate both means and explain the assumption behind the offset.
  4. In the hand-worked logistic fit, explain why the first weights are all one quarter and why the x=1x=1 coefficient does not have a finite unpenalised maximum.
  5. On the 342 penguin mass observations, explain why the species-by-island interaction has fewer estimable combinations than columns. Why does a full-rank additive model not prove causal species effects?
  6. The real salamander model has a Pearson dispersion statistic above one. Name two different model assumptions that could be responsible, and one check or revision for each. Why is an observed zero not a verified absence?
  7. A colleague fits log⁡Y∼N(m,s2)\log Y\sim N(m,s^2) and reports eme^m as the arithmetic mean. State the correction when the conditional log variance is s2s^2, and explain what additional assumption was used.
  8. A site survey selects a penalty using all data before splitting into training and test sets. Explain the information leak and the appropriate place for tuning. Contrast a random visit split with holding out whole sites.

18.1.1 Outline Solutions

  1. The reference mean is 16 and restored mean is 17, so the contrast is 1. The intercept 12 is the reference mean at x=0x=0, whether or not that point is well represented by data.
  2. Baseline odds are 1/31/3; multiplying by three gives odds 1 and probability 1/21/2. The probability doubles, not triples.
  3. The means are 0.8 and 3.2. The offset assumes expected count is proportional to positive exposure, conditional on the other predictors.
  4. At zero coefficients, each probability is one half and its Bernoulli variance is one quarter. Every x=1x=1 outcome is a success, so increasing its log odds continues to improve that group’s likelihood towards its boundary.
  5. Several species–island combinations have no observations, and their interaction columns cannot all be independently estimated. Additivity permits a numerical fit using observed overlap; it is an assumption, not a randomised comparison or a guarantee against confounding.
  6. A wrong mean–variance relation suggests checking simulated counts or considering a negative-binomial model; shared site conditions suggest site-level residual checks and a grouped model or validation. Other failures can coexist. A zero may be non-detection of an animal that is present.
  7. Under conditional lognormality the arithmetic mean is em+s2/2e^{m+s^2/2}. Without that distributional assumption, the same correction need not apply; eme^m is not generally the arithmetic mean.
  8. The chosen penalty has used test outcomes and the test score is no longer a clean evaluation of the full selection procedure. Tune within training data using a split appropriate to the intended prediction; hold whole sites out when the target is a new site.

18.2 Count Extensions, Categorical and Bayesian Models

Work through the calculations before consulting the solutions. In each applied answer state the population, observational unit and assumptions as well as the numerical result.

  1. A three-category multinomial model has reference-category weight 1 and other weights 2 and 3. Calculate all category probabilities. If the first non-reference weight doubles while the others are unchanged, calculate the new probabilities and explain what happens to the other categories.

  2. An ordinal model has thresholds −1-1 and 11 and predictor η=1\eta=1. Calculate the cumulative probabilities and the three category probabilities. In the convention used here, what happens to the odds of a category at or below either threshold if η\eta increases by one?

  3. A prior is Beta⁡(2,2)\operatorname{Beta}(2,2) and seven of ten comparable visits produce a detection. Derive the posterior, its mean and the probability of a detection at one more comparable visit. Explain why this does not establish occupancy.

  4. In the hierarchical example, explain why the site with one detection in ten is not simply assigned its raw proportion, and name two assumptions to vary in a sensitivity analysis.

  5. A fitted zero-inflated count model matches the observed fraction of zero counts. A colleague concludes that the mixture component represents sites where the species is truly absent. Give two alternative explanations and one design or measurement that could help distinguish them.

  6. A posterior sampler has 100,000 retained draws, high acceptance and visually similar chain means, but a lag-one correlation of 0.99. Explain what remains uncertain and how you would evaluate numerical precision before reporting a tail probability.

  7. A repeated-site count model has a nonlinear mean, an NB2 conditional distribution and a random site intercept. Explain which component addresses the gradient, extra conditional count variation and within-site dependence. How should you evaluate prediction for new sites?

18.2.1 Outline Solutions

  1. The original probabilities are (2/6,3/6,1/6)=(1/3,1/2,1/6)(2/6,3/6,1/6)=(1/3,1/2,1/6). With weights (4,3,1)(4,3,1) they are (1/2,3/8,1/8)(1/2,3/8,1/8). The other probabilities change because all weights share the same normalising denominator.
  2. The cumulative probabilities are F(−2)≈0.119F(-2)\approx0.119 and F(0)=0.5F(0)=0.5; subtracting gives approximately (0.119,0.381,0.5)(0.119,0.381,0.5). The lower-tail cumulative odds at each threshold are multiplied by e−1e^{-1}.
  3. The posterior is Beta⁡(9,5)\operatorname{Beta}(9,5) and its mean is 9/14≈0.6439/14\approx0.643. The posterior predictive probability on one further comparable visit is also 9/149/14. The model describes detections under a common probability, not the chance of presence when detection is imperfect.
  4. The model combines that site’s likelihood with a shared distribution learned from all four sites. Vary the fixed concentration and the hyperprior, and check the assumptions of comparable independent visits and the form of site heterogeneity.
  5. Repeated sampling with imperfect detection and unmodelled site heterogeneity are alternatives; so are inappropriate effort assumptions or a different count distribution. Repeated visits with a documented detection protocol or independent presence evidence can help, provided the design and observation assumptions support that inference.
  6. High autocorrelation can make the effective information far smaller than the raw draw count, and similar chain means do not rule out missed modes or poorly explored tails. Use vetted split-Rhat, bulk and tail effective sample sizes, trace and rank plots, and a Monte Carlo standard error appropriate to the tail probability; compare an independent calculation when feasible. Passing a numerical diagnostic still does not validate the model.
  7. The smooth represents the gradient in the conditional mean, NB2 allows extra count variation conditional on the site effect, and the shared intercept induces dependence between visits after it is integrated out. Hold entire sites out and integrate over a new site effect for the stated prediction. The design must contain enough sites and within-site replication to distinguish the components; none identifies detection on its own.
